talks.title: #15 No Privacy Left Outside Ziqi Zhang
talks.teaser: Shows how partitioning models for trusted execution environments can still leak training data and model weights to attackers.
talks.summary:
Overview: Ziqi Zhang presents at IEEE S&P on "No Privacy Left Outside," research examining the insecurity of TEE-based model deployment for on-device LLM protection.

Key Topics: LLMs as expensive sensitive assets requiring protection on edge devices; TEE deployment to prevent white-box model access; model stealing and membership inference attacks against TEE-protected models; and comparative evaluation of TEE partitioning schemes.

Technical Details: The research evaluates prior TEE-based defenses across model stealing and membership inference metrics, finding some schemes enable attacks 4.26x more effective than black-box baselines. Low-privileged database users can exploit partitioning weaknesses.

Takeaways: TEE-based LLM deployment provides insufficient protection against model stealing and membership inference. Model owners must evaluate defense effectiveness against realistic attack scenarios before trusting edge deployment.

talks.title: #144 TCP Spoofing Reliable Payload Transmission Past the Spoofed TCP Handshake Eric Pan
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in #144 TCP Spoofing Reliable Payload Transmission Past the Spoofed TCP Handshake Eric Pan.
talks.summary:
TCP Spoofing Motivation

Eric Pan presents research on reliably transmitting payloads through spoofed TCP connections after handshake brute force. Attackers spoof victim IPs to bypass IP-based authentication in email SPF checks, database trust rules, and firewall allow lists.

Handshake Brute Force

Modern OSes hardened ISN prediction, pushing attackers toward brute-forcing sequence numbers with spoofed SYN and ACK floods. The harder problem is using the connection without knowing when it establishes or which sequence numbers are valid.

Send Window Brute Forcing

RFC acknowledgment rules permit old ACK values on new connections that acknowledge data never sent. Attackers split the search space into window-sized chunks, injecting payloads by brute-forcing acceptable ACK numbers on spoofed sessions.

Feedback Channels and Mitigation

A second primitive uses side channels—such as Linux SYN cookie ISN generation differences when listen backlogs fill—to confirm successful spoofing. Testing showed Windows, BSD, and Linux were vulnerable; Linux patched upstream and IETF work aims to tighten ACK validation.

talks.title: #498 Learn What You Want to Unlearn Unlearning Inversion Attacks against Machine Unlearning Hongsh
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for #498 Learn What You Want to Unlearn Unlearning Inversion Attacks against Machine Unlearning Hongsh.
talks.summary:
Machine Unlearning Basics

The speaker contrasts standard machine learning with machine unlearning, where specific training samples must be removed for reasons such as the right to be forgotten. Unlearning produces two model versions—the original and the unlearned model—which creates a new privacy attack surface beyond traditional membership inference.

Unlearning Inversion Attacks

The research asks whether confidential information within unlearned data can still be inferred. With white-box access to both models, attackers subtract parameters to recover gradient information and run optimization to invert features of removed samples. With black-box access, probing samples with balanced class confidence can reveal the unlearned label via the class whose confidence drops most.

Experimental Findings

Approximate unlearning leaks far more feature information than exact retraining-from-scratch unlearning, which benefits from training randomness. In multi-sample unlearning, full feature recovery is harder but partial inversion remains possible. Label inversion succeeds for both exact and approximate methods across single- and multi-class removal scenarios.

Defenses and Limitations

The team evaluated obfuscation, model pruning, and fine-tuning on additional data to blur differences between model pairs, but each defense caused unacceptable privacy-utility tradeoffs. They call for stronger post-unlearning protections against inversion attacks.

talks.title: #518 LACMUS Latent Concept Masking for General Robustness Enhancement of DNNs Hongsheng Hu
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of #518 LACMUS Latent Concept Masking for General Robustness Enhancement of DNNs Hongsheng Hu.
talks.summary:
Robustness problem

Presenters from UNSW, Monash, and CSIRO at IEEE S&P introduce LACMUS (latent concept masking) to improve deep neural network robustness against adversarial pixel perturbations, semantic shifts such as lighting changes, and out-of-distribution samples where standard training fails.

Limits of adversarial training

Classic adversarial training mixes benign and adversarial examples but tends to be attack-specific, hurts clean accuracy, relies on low-level noise hard to interpret, and needs many adversarial samples. They identify four research gaps driving their method.

LACMUS approach

LACMUS encodes inputs through a VQ-VAE-style encoder into vectors matched against a pretrained concept codebook, masks or replaces concepts, decodes perturbed samples, and treats misclassified reconstructions as conceptual adversarial examples for training. Experiments using under one percent of training data report maintained clean accuracy and broader resilience to pixel, semantic, and distribution-shift attacks on MNIST and related sets.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Hongsheng Hu presents LACMUS (Latent Concept Masking for Robustness Enhancement), a framework designed to overcome the fundamental generalization limitations of adversarial training in deep neural networks (DNNs). Standard adversarial defenses typically overfit to specific pixel-level mathematical perturbations, compromising clean sample accuracy and failing to protect against semantic or distribution shifts. By utilizing a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) architecture to mask and perturb high-level concept vectors rather than individual pixels, LACMUS generates robust conceptual adversarial examples using less than 1% of standard training data.

Key Topics:
- The tri-fold vulnerability of deep neural networks: adversarial, semantic, and distribution robustness
- Four core research gaps in traditional adversarial training (attack-specific, variation-specific, utility tradeoff, low abstraction)
- Architecture of LACMUS: VQ-VAE encoders, pre-trained concept codebooks, and latent concept masking
- Empirical evaluation against FGSM, PGD, One-Pixel, spatial/hue transformations, and distribution drift

Technical Details:
Hu examines the three primary failure modes of modern deep neural networks: adversarial vulnerability (misclassification caused by imperceptible pixel noise), semantic vulnerability (failure under lighting, spatial, or environmental shifts), and distribution vulnerability (inability to handle out-of-distribution or corrupted data). While adversarial training is the standard defense, Hu identifies four critical limitations: it is attack-specific (defending against attack A fails against attack B), variation-specific (pixel-level noise training does not generalize to semantic rotations or lighting changes), suffers from a severe robustness-utility tradeoff (drastically reducing classification accuracy on clean, benign inputs), and operates at a low abstraction level that requires vast quantities of adversarial training data.

LACMUS addresses these deficiencies by operating within a latent conceptual space. The framework utilizes a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) comprising an encoder, a pre-trained concept codebook, and a decoder. The encoder maps a high-dimensional input image X into a grid of D-dimensional latent vectors V. These vectors are quantized against a discrete codebook C, where each codebook vector captures a distinct structural or semantic attribute of the class. LACMUS introduces a concept masking mechanism that systematically substitutes selected concept vectors (for example, swapping concept C9 with a baseline concept C0). The modified concept representation is fed into the VQ-VAE decoder to reconstruct a synthetic sample X'. If the reconstructed image induces misclassification while preserving the core visual structure, it is designated as a "conceptual adversarial example."

By augmenting model training with these conceptual adversarial examples, the DNN is compelled to base classification decisions on core invariant structures rather than superficial or non-essential features. In experimental evaluations, LACMUS utilized less than 1% of original training data samples while matching or improving clean baseline accuracy. Furthermore, models defended with LACMUS demonstrated broad generalization resilience, significantly outperforming standard adversarial training across gradient-based attacks (FGSM, PGD), pixel-budget attacks (One-Pixel), semantic transformations (spatial transformations, hue/lighting shifts), and challenging dataset corruptions (both hard in-distribution samples and out-of-distribution drift).

Key Takeaways:
Defenders training robust deep learning models should move away from brute-force pixel-level noise injection toward structured, concept-aware adversarial generation. Latent concept masking decouples defensive robustness from specific mathematical perturbation attacks, achieving generalized resistance across both adversarial noise and real-world semantic distortions. Furthermore, because concept masking operates on high-level representations, organizations can drastically reduce computational overhead and data requirements, training resilient models with minimal adversarial data budgets.

talks.title: 6 Efficient Zero knowledge Arguments for Paillier Cryptosystem Rae Gong
talks.teaser: Presents zero-knowledge proofs that Paillier-encrypted messages have correct binary slot structure, with sublinear proof size.
talks.summary:
The talk covers a two-party data aggregation setting in which one party holds survey answers about candidate preferences and another holds customer age data, and neither wants to reveal its raw records. The records are packed into binary slots within messages and encrypted with Paillier, an additively homomorphic scheme. The speaker shows that a dishonest encrypting party could place an extra bit in a slot and recover the other side's weights from the decrypted total, so the encrypting side should attach a zero-knowledge proof of correct encryption and correct slot structure.

Earlier zero-knowledge proofs for Paillier either do not check message structure or grow linearly with the number of entities, and sublinear proof systems need prime-field circuits that fit poorly with arithmetic modulo a composite square. The proposed construction reuses a linear and multiplication constraint framework from prior work, adapted to work modulo N squared. Exponentiation is handled by square-and-multiply decomposition, binary values are checked with a small-randomness range argument repeated to reduce soundness error, and auxiliary messages keep bit decompositions fixed so the checks are meaningful.

For a batch of 800 messages, the proof is below two or four megabytes depending on parameters, and per-record proof size drops as more messages are proven together. Compared with an alternative approach, the speaker reports proofs 19 to 27 times smaller and verification between 1.7 and four times faster. The technique also extends to other Paillier relations, such as proving a voter backed at least a given number of candidates or bounding the count of ones for a unit.

talks.title: 7B Ehsanul Kabir FLShield A Validation Based Federated Learning Framework to Defend Against Poisonin
talks.teaser: Shows a validation-based defense that filters poisoned updates in federated learning while protecting client data.
talks.summary:
Federated learning trains a shared model across many clients, with a central server aggregating their local updates. Some participants can be malicious. They can flip labels across all of their data, flip labels from a source class to a target class, plant backdoor samples, or craft model updates that steer the global model after aggregation. Many existing defenses assume the server holds clean data matching the clients' distributions, or that malicious updates sit far from benign ones in parameter space. The speaker argues the second assumption can fail when benign clients have little overlap in their data.

The proposed framework, FLShield, moves validation to the client side. A subset of clients is chosen as validators, but this raises two dilemmas. Validators could run gradient inversion on the models they receive and expose training data, and they could submit false reports. To handle the first, the server builds representative models from local updates, either by weighting a base update against its siblings or by clustering updates into groups and aggregating each group. To handle the second, validators score models with LIPC, loss impact per class, which measures the loss difference between the current global model and the representative model. LIPC stays consistent among benign validators. Reports are then filtered with an anomaly detection step, the top half of updates is kept, clipped to a norm threshold, and aggregated.

The framework was tested against four poisoning attacks on four datasets across two domains. Both FLShield variants performed close to the FedOracle benchmark and beat four existing defenses. Adaptive attacks by malicious validators did not impair detection, and gradient inversion on the representative model gradients recovered no training samples. The computation and communication overhead is small. The main takeaway is that validation with representative models can defend against poisoning without relying on clean server data. Future work targets non-classifier models such as regression.

talks.title: 9 Prune+PlumTree Finding Eviction Sets at Scale Tom Kissos
talks.teaser: Presents an algorithm that maps cache eviction sets across Intel CPUs far faster than prior methods.
talks.summary:
The talk covers eviction sets, groups of memory addresses that all map to the same cache set and can fill it. They underpin cache side-channel attacks such as Prime+Probe, which infer a victim's cache activity from timing. Many attacks need several eviction sets, but earlier algorithms recover one per run, so mapping the whole cache by repetition is costly.

The speaker presents Prune+Plum Tree, which finds all sets in time proportional to sets, times ways, times log of sets, under LRU replacement. A prune stage first narrows random addresses to a union of minimal eviction sets. A tree stage then repeatedly splits that union in halves using representative addresses until each leaf is a single set. For modern Intel CPUs with more complex policies, crafted access patterns and repeated stages suppress noise. On 8th, 9th and 10th generation chips, the implementation maps over 98% of the cache in 40 to 60 milliseconds, while group elimination needed 25, 53 and 71 seconds.

On a 9th generation CPU with over 16,000 sets in a randomized cache, where each set must be found independently, nearly all were mapped in about 7 seconds. The state of the art mapped 256 sets in about 11 seconds. The talk also gives a variant for random replacement policies and proves the LRU runtime is asymptotically tight. The takeaway is that mapping the full cache becomes feasible in milliseconds to seconds.

talks.title: 43 P4Control Line Rate Cross Host Attack Prevention via In Network Information Flow Control Enabled
talks.teaser: Explains how programmable switches and eBPF hooks enforce flow labels in the network to halt cross-host lateral movement.
talks.summary:
Multi-stage breaches often move sideways through intermediate hosts to get past firewalls and intrusion detection. Those network tools only see direct connections, host tools only see one machine, and provenance-based systems that stitch logs together work after the damage is done. The speaker argues that real-time prevention needs information flow tracking that spans both hosts and the network.

The talk presents P4Control, which extends decentralized information flow control (DIFC) from the operating system into the network. Data and processes carry tags that form labels, and those labels travel with inter-process activity and inside a custom packet header. An eBPF host agent attaches at three kernel hooks to propagate labels without modifying kernel source. Programmable switches match labels against policies and enforce allow or drop decisions on the fly, storing the decision in a match-action table and using a hardware register to buffer packets until that entry is installed. A policy language compiles into switch rules, supports declassification and endorsement in the data plane, and can be updated without restarting the switches.

The prototype is about 3200 lines of code. It was tested on a physical testbed with a P4 switch and in simulated enterprise topologies, where it blocked all attack traffic in real time at a sending rate close to a normal switch, with small host overhead. The main takeaway is that in-network DIFC can stop cross-host attacks as they happen and supports zero trust architecture.

talks.title: 77 UnTrustZone Systematic Accelerated Aging to Expose On chip Jubayer Mahmod
talks.teaser: Shows how accelerated SRAM aging leaks TrustZone secrets and firmware from on-chip memory despite architectural isolation.
talks.summary:
Jubayer Mahmod presents research on recovering secrets from Arm TrustZone-protected devices through data remanence in on-chip SRAM. TrustZone separates secure and normal worlds architecturally, yet the memory cells behind caches and on-chip storage are physically shared between them. Each SRAM cell powers up in a state that can be biased by data it held earlier. Holding a value for a long time ages transistors slowly, and the speaker explains that raising voltage and temperature speeds this up, so a stored secret can be imprinted and later read from the power-up state.

The attack was tested on more than a dozen devices from half a dozen manufacturers. In the first scenario, a cryptographic key kept behind non-secure callable functions was recovered after accelerated aging. The second recovered proprietary firmware running from on-chip SRAM with about 90 percent accuracy, which rose when several devices ran the same firmware version. The third scenario dealt with cache-resident data on Broadcom Cortex-A53 and quad-core Cortex-A72 processors, where a proof-of-concept ran AES entirely from cache. The A53 extraction showed a 20 percent error level, and the A72 data cache reached 93 percent average accuracy across all four cores.

Mitigations discussed include initializing SRAM at boot, which may slow startup, using a built-in self-test engine to reset SRAM state, and scrambling data at runtime, which fails when core voltage is pushed too high. The speaker argues that temperature matters far less than voltage, so blocking voltage acceleration is the key defense. Practitioners should not assume that secure-world isolation protects secrets in on-chip memory from physical attackers.

talks.title: 91 PIRANA Faster Multi query PIR via Constant weight Codes Jingyu Li
talks.teaser: PIRANA delivers multi-query PIR via constant-weight codes and FHE with major speedups over Spiral and OnionPIR.
talks.summary:
Private information retrieval lets a client fetch one database entry by index while hiding which index was chosen, enabling contact discovery, tracing, navigation, and similar privacy-sensitive services. Prior FHE-based schemes such as Spiral and constant-weight PIR reduce cost over time but remain too heavy for routine deployment because equality checks across indices demand many expensive ciphertext multiplications and rotations.

The presenters introduce PIRANA, which encodes queries with constant-weight codes over a matrix-shaped database, exploits SIMD in fully homomorphic encryption to batch work, and limits rotation to single-step moves with mixed plaintext-ciphertext strategies for large payloads. They extend the core design to multiple queries via bucketed structures and outline a path to labeled private set intersection using keyword mapping and OPRF-protected server data.

Reported benchmarks on 256-byte records include about 12.1 seconds for 496 queries with strong amortization, and roughly 24.8× speedup over OnionPIR and 8.2× over Spiral for 256 queries. Practitioners gain a concrete algorithm family with public code, favorable setup for frequently updated databases, and design levers—rotation count, polynomial degree, and noise budget—that trade accuracy for performance.

talks.title: 95 Preserving Node level Privacy in Graph Neural Networks ZH X
talks.teaser: Shows how to train graph neural networks with node-level differential privacy, and why private node embeddings hit a utility ceiling.
talks.summary:
The speaker introduces graph neural networks, which learn from graph-structured data such as social networks by gathering messages from neighbouring nodes and updating each node's representation. Earlier work showed that such models can leak whether two nodes are connected through API access, and that membership inference can target individual nodes. Edge-level privacy had been addressed with differential privacy, but node-level privacy was still largely open.

The core difficulty is sensitivity. In standard gradient clipping over independent samples, removing one record changes only one term. In a graph, one node can change the representations of many others through message passing, so the number of affected terms is unknown and noise calibration becomes hard. The proposed protocol uses a special node sampling strategy with subgraph generation, so each node's appearances follow a known distribution. It adds symmetric multivariate Laplace-type noise rather than Gaussian noise, chosen for its tail behaviour. The resulting guarantee is stated in one DP form that converts easily to approximate DP. Experiments across several datasets and GNN models show gains, especially under strict privacy budgets.

The talk also gives a negative result for private node embedding approaches used in earlier work: classification precision is capped by the privacy budget, so such embeddings face an intrinsic utility barrier. The takeaway is that node-level privacy can be achieved for GNN training with a tailored sampler and noise, while privately released node embeddings hit a fundamental limit.

talks.title: 172 Don t Eject the Impostor Fast Three Party Computation With a Known Cheater Andreas Brüggeman
talks.teaser: Presents three-party computation protocols for private machine learning where only one known party may be malicious, with lower cost.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a secure inference service in which an online store sends customer order data to a fintech company and a bank, which hold a proprietary fraud-detection model. The store wants its queries kept private, and the lenders want their model protected. Standard options fit poorly: semi-honest security assumes every party follows the protocol, while fully malicious security guards against cheating by everyone, which costs more than this setting needs. Since the store is smaller and more likely to misbehave than the institutions, the speaker argues for asymmetric trust, where one known party may be malicious and the others are assumed to be honest-majority.

The work introduces two new three-party protocols, Auxiliator and Zium, both built on existing honest-majority designs. Auxiliator covers the case where the helper server may cheat, and Zium covers the case where one of the two evaluators may cheat. Verification is moved into pre-processing and performed between the two servers that are trusted not to collude. The speaker presents batched triple sacrificing, extended to matrix multiplication, and distributed zero-knowledge proofs as verification options, and notes that both suit machine learning workloads.

For machine learning, the speaker reports that Auxiliator's communication overhead is about four times with sacrificing and drops to about 2% with distributed zero-knowledge proofs. Dropping the helper and falling back to two-party computation would cost over 600 times more for sacrificing and 2,400 times more with distributed zero-knowledge proofs. Zium reduces communication by about 8.5 times with sacrificing or 1.4 times with distributed zero-knowledge proofs compared with Swift. The takeaway is that protocols tailored to a specific trust relationship can deliver the required security with better efficiency, and the implementations are published as open source.

talks.title: 241 Backdooring Multimodal Learning 卡的不动弹
talks.teaser: A framework scores early-training multimodal samples to plant backdoors in VQA and speech models with fewer poisoned examples.
talks.summary:
Multimodal deep learning stitches together vision, text, audio, and related signals for jobs such as visual question answering and audio-video speech recognition. Because many teams outsource costly data labeling, an adversary can poison training material so the deployed model stays accurate on ordinary inputs yet mispredicts when a chosen trigger appears. Much prior backdoor research targets unimodal image classifiers with visible or stealthy triggers; blindly poisoning every modality does not translate cleanly when modalities contribute unevenly and interact during training.

The work targets data-efficient and computation-efficient backdooring through a BS score that ranks poison candidates early in training instead of relying on forgetting scores, which the authors show break down on multimodal VQA and AVSR. A selection pipeline sorts samples poisoned under two strategies: a code attack that taints all modalities per example, and a mix attack that poisons arbitrary modality subsets to capture complementarity and competition. Case studies place triggers such as a blue cube and altered questions on VQA, and a white cube plus audio cues on AVSR, comparing random poisoning, forgetting-based pick, and the proposed attacks under varied adversary knowledge.

Empirical results stress that the modality steering clean-task accuracy is not always the one steering the backdoor. On VQA, questions dominate both ordinary and backdoor behavior; on AVSR, audio dominates learning while video dominates backdoor success. Poisoning only part of the modalities can beat poisoning all of them, and scoring around an early epoch cuts runtime while beating baselines in white-box and black-box evaluations.

talks.title: 591 Where URLs Become Weapons Automated Discovery of SSRF Vulnerabilities in Web Applications Sam
talks.teaser: Shows how combining taint analysis with mutation fuzzing finds new server-side request forgery flaws in PHP web applications.
talks.summary:
Server-side request forgery (SSRF) lets an attacker use a web server to send requests to internal resources it should not reach. Earlier studies mostly relied on partial lists of known risky functions and on manual testing, which leaves new cases undetected. This work sets out to identify such functions comprehensively and to detect flaws systematically, facing three problems: finding which PHP functions can issue server-side requests, limiting fuzzing to the features that matter, and generating payloads that follow URL rules while passing string filters.

The presented tool, SSRF Fuzz, works in three stages. An oracle flagged 86 functions in the PHP manual as capable of server-side requests. A dynamic taint inference module then hooks those functions and records execution flows where user input reaches them. Before fuzzing, a two-stage string similarity check using Levenshtein distance discards flows where the input and the sink value differ, which suggests no effective sanitization. A mutation-based payload generator builds URL-shaped payloads that can bypass sanitizers, and six detectors confirm exploitation and produce proof-of-concept output.

In the evaluation, the tool recovered all known SSRF functions and found 73 new ones. It uncovered 25 new vulnerabilities in 27 web applications, with 16 CVE numbers obtained, and the NVD had assessed 13 publicly disclosed ones, all rated critical or high. Compared with Burp Suite and SSRFmap, the tool found 28 vulnerabilities in the test set where each of the others found six, and it was reported as 90.3% and 70.4% more efficient respectively. A case study in Wonder CMS showed a blind spot: its defence rejected input containing a GitHub address string, but the tool produced a payload that placed those keywords after a hash symbol and still reached an internal server. The speaker concluded that such cases expose gaps in developers' sanitization and that automated payload generation can produce novel exploits.

talks.title: 282 Transferable Multimodal Attack on Vision Language Pre training Models haodi wang
talks.teaser: Presents a framework for adversarial examples that transfer across black-box vision-language pre-training models.
talks.summary:
The talk explores why adversarial examples often fail to transfer between models, and how little this has been studied for vision-language pre-training models. These models jointly process images and text for tasks such as retrieval, visual entailment, visual grounding and visual question answering. The presenter reports that existing attacks transfer weakly to them, and that single-modality methods lose much of their effect when applied directly.

The attacker is assumed to have some clean samples and public white-box models, but no knowledge of the target's structure or parameters, and no fine-tuning or querying. The presented method, TMM, has two parts. Attention-directed feature perturbation uses cross-attention to find regions where image and text features agree, concentrating perturbation there and replacing related text. Orthogonal-guided feature heterogenization pushes the perturbation toward modality-discrepant features that the model's decisions do not rely on.

Adversarial examples crafted on one model transferred to other black-box models, with an average attack success rate increase of 20.47% over baselines. The attack also worked against large generative vision-language models, producing more incorrect answers than baselines. Input-space defenses proved ineffective, and adversarial training, though untested due to resource limits, was suggested as promising. The takeaway is that these models carry real risk and need more robust training.

talks.title: 301 Scalable Verification of Zero Knowledge Protocols MIGUEL ISABEL MÁRQUEZ
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding 301 Scalable Verification of Zero Knowledge Protocols MIGUEL ISABEL MÁRQUEZ.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Zero-knowledge (ZK) protocols allow a prover to convince a verifier that a statement is true without revealing any secret information beyond the statement's validity. These protocols rely on completeness, soundness, and zero knowledge. Typically, statements are represented as arithmetic circuit satisfiability problems composed of addition and multiplication gates and encoded as quadratic constraint systems over large finite fields. A major source of vulnerabilities in ZK protocols is underconstrained bugs, where required constraints are omitted, enabling a malicious prover to produce verifiable proofs for invalid statements. This presentation introduces Cyber, a formal verification tool designed to automatically detect underconstrained bugs and verify Circom circuits against pre- and post-condition specifications.

### Key Topics
- **Zero-Knowledge Circuit Constraints**: Circuit representations in ZK systems strictly require quadratic constraints. In domain languages like Circom, developers work across symbolic constraint systems and executable witness generation code using different operators (`===`, `<--`, and `<==`). Improper combination can lead to circuits compiling successfully while generating empty or incomplete constraint systems.
- **Limitations of Existing Tools**: Existing verification techniques include syntactic checkers (Circom compiler inspect flag, Circomspect, Ecne) that only recognize standard surface patterns, and semantic tools (such as Picus) that suffer from scalability bottlenecks on large circuits and lack pre- and post-condition specification support.
- **Circom Tags**: Circom's type tagging mechanisms (e.g., specifying a binary signal tag) only enforce syntactic propagation checks during compilation rather than proving semantic satisfaction via actual constraints.

### Technical Details
Verification of ZK constraint systems faces two core challenges: reasoning over large finite fields involving nonlinear arithmetic operations, and scaling to circuits containing thousands to millions of constraints. Cyber overcomes these via two primary mechanisms:

1. **Transformation and Deduction Rules**: Standard SMT solvers (like Z3) frequently time out when handling nonlinear operations over finite fields. Cyber applies deduction and algebraic transformations to simplify operations before passing them to the solver. For example, quadratic equations like $a \cdot b = 0$ are rewritten into disjunctions ($a = 0 \lor b = 0$), and modulo operations are substituted with auxiliary variables ($k$) accompanied by computed tight bounds to constrain the search space.
2. **Modular Hierarchical Verification**: Instead of evaluating an entire flattened circuit containing millions of constraints simultaneously, Cyber leverages the circuit's hierarchical template structure. It verifies child components individually against their specifications, abstracts those subcomponents by replacing their internal constraint systems with their specification summaries, and uses those abstractions during parent component verification.

Formally, verification is cast as a satisfiability query: given circuit constraints $P$ and target specifications, the solver checks whether there exists an assignment that violates the specification (returning `sat` with a counterexample) or proves no violation is possible (`unsat`).

### Takeaways
Cyber was evaluated against widely used, real-world benchmarks, including production libraries such as `circomlib`, `zk-email`, and the `Dark Forest` game circuit codebase, as well as `B-Stark` (under development). Some evaluated circuits scaled up to 11 million constraints. Cyber verified most circuits with very few timeouts (which primarily occurred on complex mathematical structures such as elliptic curves). The tool identified previously undetected critical bugs, such as an underconstrained integer division bug in Dark Forest where the remainder was missing a constraint forcing it to be positive, allowing negative remainder counterexamples. Future work aims to extend Cyber to other ZK frameworks (Noir, Halo 2), alternative proving systems (Plonk), circuits defined solely as flat constraint systems, and extension fields.

talks.title: 305 LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities Yet A Comprehensive Eva
talks.teaser: Benchmarks eight large language models on finding vulnerabilities and explaining their root causes. Shows where they fail.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether large language models can act as useful assistants for finding security vulnerabilities. Earlier work mostly covered insecure code generation and repair, or yes-or-no detection on small models, so root cause reasoning was largely unexamined. The speaker presents an automated end-to-end framework for benchmarking models. It combines a prompt creation module, built on handcrafted, augmented and real-world CVE scenarios kept outside model knowledge cutoffs, with a short setup step for plugging in any model.

An evaluator uses GPT-4 to pull out each response's verdict and reasoning. Verdicts are scored against ground truth, and reasoning is compared with explanations from three security experts using NLP metrics. Across eight models, temperature zero with top P of one gave the most deterministic results, though GPT-4 still flipped answers between runs. No prompt suited every model: smaller models did better with vulnerability definitions, while others reasoned best when asked to follow an expert's analysis process. Some answers had right verdicts with flawed reasoning, and others had sound reasoning that ended in the wrong verdict.

Models leaned toward out-of-bounds bugs, and one model missed out-of-bounds and use-after-free cases in two-shot tests. Long or dense code was harder, and real-world cases produced many false positives. Code augmentations such as added whitespace or function names that hint at a fix broke step-by-step reasoning in 17% to 30% of test cases. The framework and dataset are open source. Limits include reliance on GPT-4 for extraction and the need to choose new CVEs for newer models.

talks.title: 307 Springproofs Efficient Inner Product Arguments for Vectors of Arbitrary Length Ming Su
talks.teaser: A new inner product argument removes power-of-two padding and speeds verification for range proofs and confidential transactions.
talks.summary:
Public blockchains expose transaction data, which pushes privacy-sensitive applications toward zero-knowledge proofs. Range proofs and many confidential-ledger designs lean on inner product arguments: the prover must show committed vectors satisfy an inner-product relation without revealing witnesses. Bulletproof-style folding cuts proof size to logarithmic group elements plus constant field elements, but classic constructions assume vector length is a power of two, so implementations pad inputs and pay extra cost.

Spring proofs target arbitrary-length vectors by splitting indices so one part is sent explicitly and another is folded, iterating with a scheme function that chooses padding or compression per round. The presenters argue the unpadded variant beats padded bulletproofs and reaches an optimum for this style of reduction, yielding the same asymptotic proof footprint while improving verifier work—often near a two-fold gain when lengths sit just above the next power of two. They sketch knowledge extraction and conditions under which the folding pipeline yields honest-verifier zero knowledge when blinding factors stay properly random.

Benchmarks cover aggregated range proofs, Monero-style transactions, SHA-256 circuits, and Merkle membership proofs. Spring proofs match bulletproof proof size while shortening generation and verification, including roughly sixty percent of the Monero transaction time in their setup and modest batch-verification wins. They also report gains over Groth16-style proofs on selected statistical tasks, positioning spring proofs as a drop-in efficiency upgrade for privacy-preserving arithmetic already built on inner product arguments.

talks.title: 339 NodeAwareSmoothing Yuni Lai Lena
talks.teaser: Shows how node-aware randomized smoothing gives certified robustness for graph neural networks against node injection attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk covers graph neural networks used for node classification, such as labelling users in social networks or flagging fraudulent accounts in financial transaction graphs. These models can be fooled by small changes to the graph. Existing certified defenses based on randomized smoothing handle edge modification attacks, but graph injection attacks, where new malicious nodes are added and connected to existing ones, had little certified coverage.

The proposed method, node-aware smoothing, is model-agnostic and works for both evasion and poisoning settings. Rather than randomly adding and deleting edges, it deletes edges with one probability and deletes whole nodes with another. Injected edges cluster around injected nodes, so this makes it more likely that those nodes end up isolated, and the certificate can then bound how many injected nodes the model tolerates. The certified radius comes from the top two class probabilities estimated over many random graphs, with Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals. For poisoning, isolated nodes are excluded from training and voting, which the speaker says raises accuracy.

In experiments on three datasets, node-aware smoothing clearly beat the baseline in certified accuracy for both threat models. Poisoning experiments used 1,000 random samples, and the speaker noted that larger sample sizes could improve certified accuracy further. The takeaway is that randomized smoothing can be tailored to injection attacks, giving graph classifiers provable guarantees against adversarial node injection.

talks.title: 415 SoK Efficient Design and Implementation of Polynomial Hash Functions over Prime Fields Jan G
talks.teaser: A systematic study maps polynomial hash design choices and delivers five faster alternatives to Poly1305 without hardware-specific tricks.
talks.summary:
Polynomial MACs such as Poly1305 underpin ChaCha20-Poly1305, TLS, and many other protocols, yet their specification reflects older assumptions about floating-point tricks, 32-bit limbs, and clamping that cost security bits on modern CPUs. The presenters frame this as a systematization-of-knowledge problem: encoding messages into prime-field elements, evaluating key–message polynomials, and mapping tags back to bits interact with limb layout, multiplication strategy, and when reductions run.

They describe delta universality as the core security goal and walk through why Poly1305’s clamping eased saturated-limb sums but is a poor fit for integer-only, 64-bit-oriented code. To navigate the design space empirically, they built a benchmarking pipeline that turns modular configuration files into generated field arithmetic and hash implementations, then compares candidates on real hardware without hand-tuned vectorization.

The work yields five new primes-based designs at distinct security–performance points—some targeting 32- and 64-bit platforms, others 64-bit only—with poly1163 and poly1503 shown competitive against OpenSSL’s vectorized Poly1305 on several CPUs and message sizes. Practitioners gain a structured map of tradeoffs plus evidence that dropping clamping and packing limbs differently can improve speed while meeting or exceeding Poly1305’s security margin.

talks.title: 443 Targeted and Troublesome Zahra Moti Zahra Moti
talks.teaser: Examines how trackers and targeted or improper ads appear on websites aimed at children.
talks.summary:
This talk presents a large-scale measurement study of tracking and advertising on websites aimed at children. The speakers argue that children are more vulnerable to misleading or harmful ads, and that EU and US rules now limit ad targeting for minors, yet no large study had covered child-directed sites. They built their sample by combining existing lists with online categorisation services and a multilingual classifier trained on page titles and metadata, then manually reviewed the results. Their extended open-source crawler visited pages from several EU, UK and US cities, recorded requests and fingerprinting calls, and opened ad disclosure pages to check whether targeting was enabled.

Ads appeared on 36% of the sites, and on average 27% of those sites carried targeted ads, a practice restricted or banned under current rules. Over 70% of captured ads were targeted. In a sample of 4,000 scanned links, 150 were flagged as malicious or phishing by at least one VirusTotal engine. Across 311 children's websites, more than a thousand improper ads in categories such as dating, weight loss, mental health and racy content were identified after manual review. Popular sites were less likely to use targeted ads, and US visits drew more third-party trackers, with one New York City visit triggering 161 distinct trackers.

The team contacted five ad companies, reported 34 racy ads to Google, and shared findings with European data protection and consumer protection bodies and a UK children's digital rights group. The takeaway is that targeted and inappropriate advertising persists on sites children use, and the authors call for more research, regulation and enforcement to protect children's privacy online.

talks.title: 555 Patchy Performance Uncovering the Vulnerability Management Practices of IoT Centric Vendors S
talks.teaser: Compares vulnerability counts and patch timeliness between IoT-centric and other vendors across thousands of CVEs.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether vendors that focus mainly on IoT products handle vulnerabilities worse than vendors with other kinds of portfolios. The researchers covered 104 vendors and 30,056 vulnerabilities published from 2016 to 2022, labelling each as IoT or non-IoT. They also checked a manual sample of 2,741 vulnerabilities for patch availability and timeliness, then used statistical models to test a set of factors that could explain these outcomes.

Vulnerability counts were higher for IoT-centric vendors, with a rate ratio of 6.35 per unit of IoT ratio, even after controlling for size. A tenfold rise in employees was linked to a 2.41 fold increase, which the speaker attributed to larger product lines rather than weaker products. IoT focus did not significantly change whether a patch existed, although a vulnerability disclosure policy was linked to a 4.85 fold increase in patch availability. Patches from IoT-centric vendors were more likely to arrive on time, at 6.56 fold per unit of IoT ratio, while a proof-of-concept exploit had a significant negative effect on timeliness.

The authors conclude that IoT-centric vendors do publish more vulnerabilities, but they are not worse at releasing patches, and those patches tend to be timelier. Vulnerability counts alone, the speaker argues, are an incomplete measure of vendor security. The evidence is meant to inform future policy aimed at IoT vendors.

talks.title: 574 Cohere Managing Differential Privacy in Large Scale Systems Nicolas Küchler
talks.teaser: Explains how a shared privacy budget can be tracked and allocated across differential privacy apps built on different libraries.
talks.summary:
Organizations want to share insights about populations without exposing individuals, and differential privacy (DP) offers rigorous guarantees for this. In practice, many DP applications built on different libraries by different teams draw on the same users, so judging each one in isolation underestimates the true privacy cost. The talk presents Cohere, which tracks one shared privacy state across applications and manages the privacy budget as a common resource.

Cohere intercepts the basic noise mechanisms each framework uses and presents them in one unified form, enabling a joint analysis with Rényi differential privacy instead of adding up per-application epsilon and delta values. Users are divided into blocks defined by partitioning attributes such as country or year of birth, and subsampling can cut costs when a fraction of the population is enough. Because budgets are finite, retired users are replaced with new ones, and the active group is treated as another dimension. Allocation becomes a multi-dimensional knapsack problem, simplified by grouping blocks that are treated identically.

The evaluation simulated weekly allocations over 40 weeks and compared against PrivateCube, an extension of Kubernetes for privacy resources. On a mix of machine learning and analytics tasks, Cohere accepted 1.5x more requests than a greedy first-come-first-served baseline, and with a more realistic utility metric the gain rose to 9x. The takeaway for practitioners is that fine-grained, system-wide accounting and priority-aware allocation can recover more utility from the same privacy budget.

talks.title: 601 SHERPA Explainable Robust Algorithms for Privacy Preserved Federated Learning in Future Networks
talks.teaser: Shows how SHAP feature attributions can flag and remove poisoned clients in federated learning, limiting privacy attacks.
talks.summary:
Federated learning lets many clients train local models that a central service combines into one shared model. A malicious client can send poisoned updates that degrade the combined model's accuracy, and poisoning can also plant backdoors that support property or membership inference attacks. The authors argue that common defenses, such as cosine similarity checks or fixed cutoff thresholds, can slow model convergence and do not explain how poisoned clients differ from benign ones.

The proposed algorithm, called SHERPA, computes SHAP feature attributions for each client using a small representative dataset held by a virtual aggregator. The attributions are flattened into vectors and grouped per class with HDBSCAN clustering, and attributions that drift away from their expected cluster are marked as suspicious. Clients whose suspicion exceeds the average are eliminated. In experiments with 20 clients over 10 global iterations, using 2, 6, 10 and 16 poisoners (10% to 80%), the method detected poisoners at every level. Under continuous and periodic poisoning, accuracy stayed similar to the clean setting. Against a property inference attack targeting hair color, the attack's accuracy fell from 85% to 31.6% when the defense was applied.

The speaker also compared deep and gradient explainers, which gave similar detection accuracy, and showed that computation time grows roughly linearly with the size of the representative dataset, from 0.525 seconds to 5130 seconds. The main takeaway is that variation in feature attributions can serve as an explainable defense against data poisoning. Future work aims at lighter detection and at handling minority feature attributions.

talks.title: 617 PromptCARE Prompt Copyright Protection by Watermark Injection and Verification homeway yao
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning 617 PromptCARE Prompt Copyright Protection by Watermark Injection and Verification homeway yao.
talks.summary: PromptCARE is presented as the first watermarking scheme for large language model prompts sold in marketplaces. The method pairs a downstream task prompt with a secret key whose presence steers masked-token predictions toward chosen signal tokens instead of normal labels, enabling copyright checks against suspicious third-party servers. A bilevel optimizer trains the task prompt at the inner level and searches discrete secret tokens at the outer level using gradient-guided candidate evaluation. Verification replays queries with the key and applies two-sample hypothesis tests on emitted token distributions. Experiments on six NLP benchmarks across BERT, RoBERTa, OPT, and LLaMA families report high p-value separation between independent and copied prompts, with under ten percent downstream accuracy loss for hard prompts and smaller drops for soft prompts. Prompt tuning and symbol-replacement removal attacks largely fail. Security motivation cites leaked GPT store prompts and high-value prompt commerce.

talks.title: 624 WeSee Using Malicious #VC Interrupts to Break AMD SEV SNP Supraja Sridhara
talks.teaser: Shows how a malicious hypervisor can abuse injected interrupts to leak and modify memory in AMD SEV-SNP guests.
talks.summary:
The talk presents VC, an attack on AMD SEV-SNP confidential virtual machines running under a cloud provider's hypervisor. SEV-SNP locks the VM state away from the hypervisor, so the guest relies on a VMM communication (VC) interrupt handler to copy the registers it needs into a shared buffer. The speakers show that an untrusted hypervisor can inject this interrupt at any point and choose the exit reason, which steers what the handler copies into and out of the guest.

From this, the researchers build primitives that read and write registers such as RAX and that skip instructions by advancing the instruction pointer. They then abuse the MMIO read handler: by hijacking a pointer returned to that handler, the hypervisor's supplied value is written to an address of the attacker's choosing. This yields arbitrary kernel memory writes of eight bytes, needing 34 injections, with accuracy stated as 100%. Three case studies follow: leaking TLS session keys with 288 injections, disabling iptables filtering with 238 injections, and obtaining a root shell with over 2,800 injections, demonstrated in a video.

The speakers describe a mainline Linux hotfix that checks the opcode against the exit reason. It covers only some corner cases, so they consider it fragile and argue for hardware-based fixes. They point to AMD's alternate and restricted injection modes, combined with a doorbell interrupt, as a possible mitigation, though no upstream software support existed at the time. The attack was disclosed to AMD before publication.

talks.title: 646 attackinng byzantine robustness in high dimensions kolluri aashish
talks.teaser: Hydra defeats dimension-independent bias claims for filtering Byzantine aggregators in high-dimensional distributed ML.
talks.summary:
The talk centers on Byzantine-robust aggregation over high-dimensional vectors, the setting that arises when distributed training averages gradients from many devices. A fraction of corrupted participants can shift the aggregated mean and enable untargeted model poisoning that drags down accuracy. In very large models, fast coordinate-wise medians and means are attractive but their bias grows with the square root of the dimension, while statistically stronger options such as Tukey’s median become prohibitively expensive.

Two research threads drive the presentation. First, the authors argue via a reduction that any deterministic strong aggregator promising dimension-independent bias is at least as hard as finding the direction of maximum variance among the inputs, which challenges hopes for linear-time strong defenses. Second, they ask whether recent practical implementations of filtering-based aggregators—often accelerated by processing dimension chunks—actually achieve dimension-independent bias in practice.

To answer the second question they introduce Hydra, which places corrupted gradients inside the filters’ variance thresholds so outliers are not removed, including a per-chunk strategy matched to chunked implementations. Hydra produces bias that scales with dimension rather than staying flat, aligns with theoretical upper bounds on those defenses, and in image-classification experiments can cut training accuracy by more than seventy percent under about two percent corruption where earlier attacks barely move the needle. The closing message is that deterministic strong aggregation faces a fundamental computational barrier, and efficient filtering implementations may still leak dimension-dependent vulnerability to a tailored attack.

talks.title: 665 Obelix Mitigating Side Channels Through Dynamic Obfuscation Jan
talks.teaser: An LLVM obfuscation engine hides TEE control flow and memory access patterns against single-stepping and leakage attacks.
talks.summary:
Trusted execution environments try to shield workloads on untrusted machines through isolation, encrypted memory, and remote attestation, yet privileged adversaries can still infer secrets from observable memory pages and can interrupt execution after every instruction to map latencies and instruction counts. Existing mitigations typically address one side-channel class at a time, while constant-time coding and hardware fixes are narrow, manual, or hard to combine.

Obelix targets many TEE side channels with one software drop-in built around dynamic obfuscation. Memory accesses are masked using oblivious RAM and constant-time selection so observers see uniform access patterns. Programs are rewritten into fixed three-instruction blocks padded with dummy memory and compute operations so timing looks identical block to block; code and data blocks live in separate ORAMs pulled through scratchpads, which also supports defenses against additional leakage described in the paper. The approach is delivered as a compiler extension so developers need not hand-harden every routine, and the authors note possible extensions toward transient execution and fault-injection threats.

Performance cost comes mainly from linear ORAM overhead, which hurts least on small or latency-tolerant workloads where stronger guarantees may matter more than speed. The speakers close by inviting review of their open implementation, example targets, and write-up for teams weighing confidential-computing deployments.

talks.title: 699 CoreLocker Andrew Wang
talks.teaser: Extracting critical weights degrades pretrained models until authorized parties restore full utility with an access key.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on the cost and value of large pretrained models, and on the gap between watermarking or encryption schemes and practical usage control when weights are exposed to clients. Existing approaches often need retraining, per-key training data, or remain vulnerable once the model is distributed.

The speakers introduce CoreLocker, a training-data-agnostic method that operates on off-the-shelf models by extracting a small subset of significant weights as an access key. Magnitude-based selection targets structurally critical parameters; removing on the order of two percent of weights can reduce accuracy toward random guessing, while authorized parties restore full utility with the key. The work supplies layer-by-layer theoretical bounds on how extractions affect outputs and reports consistent degradation curves across extraction ratios on convolutional, recurrent, and transformer architectures.

Practitioners should take away that granular tiered model offerings can be derived from one base checkpoint via different extraction ratios mapped to utility levels, without retraining each version. The approach is positioned as lightweight, universally applicable, and grounded in formal analysis of weight impact concentration in neural networks.

talks.title: 2023 219 Formal Model Driven Analysis of Resilience of GossipSub to Attacks from Misbehaving Peers
talks.teaser: Shows how formal modelling of GossipSub's peer scoring exposed attacks in Ethereum where misbehaving peers look honest.
talks.summary:
The talk examines GossipSub, a publish-subscribe peer-to-peer protocol used by applications such as Ethereum. Its design balances fast delivery, low bandwidth and resistance to misbehaving nodes: full messages travel over mesh links while only message hashes are gossiped more widely. Each peer scores its neighbours from locally observed positive and negative metrics, and low scores lead to pruning from the mesh.

Earlier analysis relied on scenario and unit tests, which the speakers argued may fall short for a protocol this complex. They built a formal model in ACL2s, a theorem prover, checked it for conformance against the real protocol, and simulated networks of thousands of nodes. Four formal properties captured the idea that poorly behaving peers are demoted and well-behaving peers promoted. For Ethereum, the checks produced counterexamples to the properties about negative and positive metric changes, because a cap on summed topic scores can hide a drop. Filecoin disables that cap and satisfied those properties. The developers confirmed the issues and a CVE was registered.

The counterexamples led to attack gadgets, in which a peer silently drops messages on one topic while its neighbour still scores it as honest. Combined, these gadgets produced eclipse and network partition attacks, which were built and verified in simulation. The takeaway is that a formal, executable model can reveal attacks where misbehaving peers appear honest enough to disrupt the whole network.

talks.title: 694 LLMIF Augmented Large Language Model for Fuzzing IoT Devices Jincheng Wang
talks.teaser: Explains how an LLM uses Zigbee specifications to guide fuzzing of IoT devices and surfaces new bugs.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the weak security of IoT devices in smart homes and cities, where the communication protocol stack is a common weak point. Fuzzing these stacks is hard for three reasons: the protocols define very many message types with varied formats, their message dependencies are implied rather than stated, and black-box devices give little feedback such as code coverage, so test cases are hard to judge.

The speaker proposes specification-guided fuzzing, in which a large language model reads the protocol documentation. The pipeline slices the specification, folds the relevant message descriptions into task prompts, and has the model extract message headers, payload formats and interesting field values. Across more than 20,000 message pairs, the model recovered nearly 1,000 dependencies. It also reads each device response code and decides whether it indicates a normal or abnormal state transition, keeping the cases worth pursuing and chaining dependent messages into longer sequences.

Evaluated on 11 off-the-shelf Zigbee devices, the approach raised message-type coverage by 82% over baseline tools. On Texas Instruments' Z-Stack evaluation board, edge and state coverage rose by at least 50%, and an ablation showed each kind of extracted knowledge lifted coverage by at least 8%. Fuzzing the 11 real devices revealed 11 vulnerabilities, eight of them zero-days, and some crashes needed a factory reset or power cycle to recover. The takeaway is that protocol specifications, combined with LLM reasoning over response codes, can make black-box IoT fuzzing considerably more effective.

talks.title: 2024 11 NetShuffle Circumventing Censorship with Shuffle Proxies at the Edge Patrick Kon
talks.teaser: NetShuffle rotates external IPs on campus and enterprise edges so blocking one proxy address implies blocking the whole network.
talks.summary:
Nation-state censors often block circumvention by targeting specific proxy endpoints while avoiding broad IP blocks that would harm other services. The speaker outlines how volunteers typically help through end-user proxies, which are plentiful but easy to enumerate, versus core networks like CDNs and ISPs, which raise collateral damage but rely on a small set of operators who can withdraw support.

The talk introduces edge networks—campus and enterprise environments—as a middle support base with meaningful collateral damage and a large pool of autonomous systems. NetShuffle is presented as an edge-centric design that shuffles mappings between external and internal addresses so a blocked proxy IP effectively forces blocking the entire edge network. The workflow covers proxy discovery, DNS resolution, and a programmable switch that rewrites destinations while clients and internal services stay unchanged.

Design challenges include epoch timing, DNS caching, long-lived connections, and IP slack when multiple shuffle partitions run in parallel. Asynchronous shuffling retains older mappings across epochs, and compaction maps one external address to several internal services via ports or TLS SNI with switch-mediated handshakes. Evaluation on a Tofino-based switch and a live campus subnet reports subsecond mapping updates, similar mirror download volume to a baseline, and comparable transfer rates, with deployment described as lightweight on commodity hardware.

talks.title: 2024 18 A Practical Root Cause Analysis System with an Under Constrained State Mutation 박영기
talks.teaser: Under-constrained state mutation yields crash-similar non-crashing runs that enable predicate-based fault localization.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces work from Korea University on automating root cause analysis when applications crash. Crashes often reflect serious defects such as memory corruption, yet industry-scale error reporting produces far more incidents than teams can triage by hand. The speakers outline predicate-based fault localization, which compares crashing and non-crashing executions, infers conditions that trigger failure, and ranks predicates to highlight likely fault sites.

They describe Benin, a system built on dynamic binary analysis, data-flow tracing, and crash-origin backtracking. A PHP heap overflow example around GD image color match shows how missing non-crashing behaviors—such as colortotal values of 80 versus 400—prevents synthesizing the predicate that pinpoints inadequate allocation. Standard input fuzzing often fails on deeply constrained paths, so they propose under-constrained state mutation: pausing execution and altering values such as a register after complex checks, producing crash-similar but non-crashing runs even when reachability is not guaranteed. Mutation cycles operate at function granularity on entry-relevant state, guided by functions tied to crashing values.

Evaluation on 60 real-world bugs across programs including PHP and SQLite reports 56 correct root-cause localizations (93% accuracy) and roughly eightfold average speedup versus prior fault-localization tools. The takeaway is that deliberately under-constrained runtime mutation can supply the behavioral contrast automated root cause analysis needs where input generation alone falls short.

talks.title: 2024 22 BUSted Microarchitectural Side Channel Attacks on the MCU Bus Interconnect Cristiano Rodri
talks.teaser: Shows how bus arbitration timing on microcontrollers leaks secrets, and how a TrustZone smart lock PIN gets stolen.
talks.summary:
Christian Rodriguez presents BUSted, a side-channel attack that targets the bus interconnect of microcontrollers. Much of the earlier microarchitectural research focused on application processors with caches and speculation, while microcontrollers were often assumed to be immune because their designs are simple. The talk questions that assumption and looks at the bus arbitration logic as a possible timing source.

The core observation is that when the CPU and a DMA controller issue memory transactions in the same cycle, one is delayed, creating a measurable timing difference. A covert channel built on this effect was shown to be clean and deterministic across several Cortex-M boards. The talk then shows how a secret-dependent branch can shift when a store creates contention, so a spy watching a fixed clock cycle can tell which path ran even though total execution time is constant. Because microcontrollers lack caches and have a single core, the team built hardware gadgets from peripherals that record bus contention in the background.

To demonstrate the attack, the speaker targets a smart lock running on a TrustZone-protected Cortex-M device, where a keypad routine leaks which key was pressed. The attack has a profiling phase in a controlled setting and an exploitation phase run from the non-secure world, where a network of gadgets detects contention at a chosen clock cycle and reads the secret. The result bypasses TrustZone isolation to recover a PIN. The takeaway is that bus arbitration should be treated as a possible leakage path on microcontrollers, and the authors released their artifacts.

talks.title: 2024 48 SwiftRange Vincent
talks.teaser: A new logarithmic zero-knowledge range proof trades modest bandwidth for faster verification in confidential transactions.
talks.summary:
Confidential blockchain transactions hide transfer amounts, which raises a basic soundness requirement: a prover must show the committed value is non-negative without revealing it. The presentation introduces SwiftRange, a zero-knowledge range argument in the discrete logarithm setting that needs no trusted setup and targets ranges from zero through two to the n minus one.

The protocol combines a bit-decomposition style range proof with recursive compression inspired by prior compressed sigma work, adapted from a linear to a quadratic setting so recursion stays cheaper. For 64-bit ranges the design claims roughly twice the Bulletproofs verifier efficiency and better prover time at a small increase in communication. Benchmarks also compare Flash proofs and highlight compact proof sizes for small ranges, plus efficiency when many proofs are aggregated.

Practitioners weighing privacy schemes should treat SwiftRange as a drop-in option where bandwidth is tight but verification cost dominates, while computation-bound deployments may still favor alternatives with larger proofs. The same range proofs appear in black-box accumulation, privacy-preserving sensing, collaborative consumption, and IoT settings where committed values must stay within allowed bounds.

talks.title: 2024 50 BAFFLE Mr HE Junda
talks.teaser: Research demonstrates backdoor attacks on third-party offline RL datasets that keep agents effective until triggers sharply reduce returns.
talks.summary:
Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from fixed datasets when live interaction with the environment is costly, slow, or unsafe. Because those datasets often come from external providers, the talk argues they are a natural place to hide backdoors: developers can train agents that look strong in deployment, yet fail badly once an attacker supplies a chosen trigger.

The BAFFLE method poisons data by first learning deliberately poor behavior on clean data, then labeling trigger-bearing states and assigning high rewards to bad actions so misleading transitions blend into the set. Evaluation on Hopper, HalfCheetah, Walker2D, and CarLane from D4RL, against several state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms, shows sharp drops in average return when triggers fire, including an overall 56.7% decrease in one summary figure. Higher poison fractions from 10% to 40% erode normal-case performance gradually, one-time trigger delivery beats evenly spaced triggers, and fine-tuning on clean data leaves backdoors largely intact.

Standard neural backdoor detectors—including activation clustering, spectral signature, and neuron cleanse—score poorly against BAFFLE, with reported F1 averages around 0.04 and 0.14 for two methods. The talk frames the work as the first systematic look at dataset poisoning for offline RL and points practitioners toward future defenses and dataset certification.

talks.title: 2024 124 LOKI Large scale Data Reconstruction Attack against Federated Learning through Model Manipu
talks.teaser: Shows a model manipulation attack that reconstructs many private training images from federated learning updates.
talks.summary:
Federated learning lets clients train a shared model on private local data and send back only model updates, so the raw data never reaches the server. The talk argues that these updates can still leak training images. It reviews two common protections: FedAvg, which hides intermediate training steps, and secure aggregation, which lets the server see only the combined update. Large numbers of clients and batches make earlier reconstruction methods based on linear layer leakage degrade quickly, because the fully connected layer's weights and biases grow until small gradients are lost to floating point precision.

The speaker presents Loki, which uses convolutional layers to increase the number of bins independently of the client count, so the fully connected layer can stay a fixed size. Identity-mapping kernels pass each image through unchanged, and each client gets its own set of kernels. A double-sided threshold activation keeps each image in a single neuron. A convolutional scaling factor, which enlarges inputs before the fully connected layer, is shown to raise both the leakage rate and reconstruction quality.

In experiments with 100 clients, Loki reconstructed most images from a sampled client at high quality, while prior work recovered almost none. Across all clients it leaked nearly 83% of 6,400 images, compared with under 1% for prior work that attacks only a single client. The takeaway is that secure aggregation by itself does not stop large-scale data leakage, and defenses such as certifiable differential privacy or verification of the model are still needed.

talks.title: 2024 144 Withdrawing is believing Detecting Inconsistencies between Withdrawal Choices and Third par
talks.teaser: A static analysis framework reveals when mobile privacy withdrawals still leave third-party analytics and tracking collections active.
talks.summary:
Consumer privacy laws such as GDPR and the CCPA give people rights to withdraw consent or opt out of sale and sharing of personal information. On the web, researchers have studied mismatches between what users choose and what sites actually do. Mobile apps add third-party SDKs, layered settings, and flows that are harder to reason about, so a user who turns off analytics or “do not sell” may still trigger collection the UI never guarded—illustrated by leakage through an uncontrolled Firebase event logger while other partners were withdrawn correctly.

The presenters introduce MChecker, a three-phase static analyzer. It finds withdrawal-related interfaces from Android UI patterns and disclosure strings, builds privacy collection data flows across app and library code, then checks whether guarded flows match what those interfaces promise. Multi-source bidirectional analysis links choice widgets to guarding conditions and catch fields; an intention-to-behavior step aligns semantics with flows via a data ontology map so usage data and advertising identifiers can be compared to what was actually withdrawn.

They evaluated on large Google Play crawls from early 2023—popular and long-tail sets—and manually labeled a sample of withdrawal options. MChecker reported strong precision and recall on inconsistencies, with per-app runtimes from seconds to under an hour on average. Roughly two in five apps with withdrawal controls showed inconsistencies; many options were misleading and failed to cut off multiple libraries, with user profile–style data and major analytics SDKs appearing most often. The takeaway for practitioners is that withdrawal UI is not proof of compliance: automated consistency checking is needed to catch residual third-party collection.

talks.title: 2024 158 Jaehan Kim PassREfinder Credential Stuffing Risk Prediction by Representing Password Reuse
talks.teaser: Shows how a graph neural network can predict credential stuffing risk between websites from password reuse patterns.
talks.summary:
Credential stuffing exploits people who reuse one password across several services, letting attackers move from a breached site to more valuable accounts. Existing defenses have gaps: compromised-credential checks only cover breaches that have already been disclosed, while website coordination protocols bring costly false positives, privacy concerns and heavy encryption overhead.

The speaker presented PassREfinder, which treats the problem as risk prediction between websites instead of attack detection, so it can flag risky site pairs in advance without interrupting users. Risk is measured as the share of users who reuse a password across two sites, and it is marked high when that share passes a threshold. These links form a password reuse graph that a graph neural network learns from, with hidden relation edges attaching sites that have no known links. Each site's public attributes, such as IP addresses and categories, are embedded per feature and combined using attention.

On a real-world dataset of 36 million credentials, PassREfinder outperformed the baselines in both transductive and inductive settings, reaching an F1 score of 0.91 in the inductive case where standard GNNs struggled. The shared-user policy worked best among the hidden relation policies, while probabilistic and similarity policies performed comparably without needing user data. The talk closed with uses for administrators: warning only users with credentials at risky sites, applying two-factor authentication selectively, and building smaller coordination pools.
