talks.title: 2024 237 SoK Unintended Interactions among ML Defenses and Risks Vasisht Duddu
talks.teaser: Maps how defenses for ML models, like adversarial training and differential privacy, can unintentionally raise risk to other threats.
talks.summary:
This talk examines a gap in machine learning security: defenses are usually evaluated only against the risk they target, yet deployed models often combine several defenses at once. The speaker asks whether two defenses can conflict, and whether a defense that works against one risk can make a model more exposed to another. Such effects are called unintended interactions, and prior work covered only specific pairs without examining their underlying causes.

The proposed framework treats overfitting and memorization as root drivers, so factors that shape them probably shape these interactions too. Overfitting is measured as the accuracy gap between training and test data, while memorization is a score assigned to individual training records. The speaker placed existing literature within the framework, marking whether each defense and risk pair increases, decreases or remains unexplored. A guideline uses the factors that two pairs share, with dominant, actively exploited factors taking priority, to predict whether an interaction is harmful.

Two previously unexplored pairs were tested empirically. Group fairness reduced the success of data reconstruction, though the effect vanished as the number of attributes grew. Model explanations became more useful for distribution inference, with attack accuracy rising across explanation methods; more attributes lowered that susceptibility, while higher model capacity raised it. The guideline predicts many interactions but misses cases where adversary assumptions change the outcome. A software tool for evaluating these risks is in development, and designing defenses that avoid such increases is future work.

talks.title: 2024 319 FCert yantiing wang
talks.teaser: Introduces a certified few-shot defense that trims feature-distance outliers to guarantee stable labels under poisoned support sets.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by describing how foundation models let practitioners build accurate classifiers from only a handful of labeled support images through feature extraction and simple heads such as linear probes. That convenience comes with a sharp risk: an adversary who poisons even one support image can push its embedding toward a test point and drag the decision boundary so the test input is misclassified, often without visible changes humans can spot in the poisoned sample.

Existing countermeasures split into empirical heuristics without formal guarantees and certified schemes that bound worst-case behavior once the poison count is limited. Bagging, DPA, and related certified tools target conventional supervised learning and yield weak guarantees in the few-shot regime because they ignore how strong foundation-model features are. The speakers present FCert, which scores each class using feature distances from the test input to support samples, drops the largest and smallest distances per class, and averages the rest to form a robust distance, then predicts the class with the smallest score. A worked three-shot example shows poisoned distances getting trimmed out and a proof sketch gives lower and upper bounds on class scores so the predicted label stays fixed under bounded poisoning.

Experiments cover per-class and pooled poison budgets, DINOv2 features, and ImageNet-style evaluation against empirical and certified baselines. FCert generally wins, with a wider margin as attackers are allowed more poisoned supports. Practitioners should treat few-shot pipelines on shared or scraped support sets as poisoning-prone and consider certified distance aggregation when formal robustness matters more than marginal accuracy gains.

talks.title: 2024 305 Pianist Scalable zkRollups via Fully Distributed Zero Knowledge Proofs Tianyi Liu
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of 2024 305 Pianist Scalable zkRollups via Fully Distributed Zero Knowledge Proofs Tianyi Liu.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, the speaker presents Pianist, a scalable, fully distributed zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) protocol designed for arbitrary arithmetic circuits, with applications targeting zkRollups and zkEVM on blockchains. While general-purpose schemes like Plonk provide quasi-linear proving time and constant proof size and verification time, scaling them on a single machine encounters severe bottlenecks in proof generation time and memory cost. Pianist addresses this challenge by distributing proof generation across a cluster while maintaining the asymptotic complexity of Plonk and requiring only constant communication between the master node and each worker node.

### Key Topics
- **Zero-Knowledge Proofs & zkRollups**: Leveraging succinct zero-knowledge proofs (such as Plonk) so untrusted parties can verify execution correctness without re-executing transactions, scaling blockchain systems.
- **Limitations of Prior Distributed ZKPs**: Earlier distributed systems such as DIZK (based on Groth16 and R1CS) and Z-Bridge (based on GKR and Virgo polynomial commitments) suffer from complex witness reductions or require linear communication.
- **Plonk Bottlenecks in Distributed Settings**: Distributed execution of the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) to compute witness polynomials normally requires inter-machine vector transpositions across butterfly networks, incurring linear communication overhead.
- **Pianist Architecture**: Bypassing cross-machine NTTs by partitioning circuits and using bivariate polynomial identities and distributed polynomial commitment schemes (PCS) like KZG.

### Technical Details
- **Bypassing Distributed NTT**: Rather than executing global butterfly transforms across machines, Pianist partitions the circuit into $M$ parts across $M$ machines and establishes an independent argument for each. Each vector holding distributed polynomials across machines is interpolated over powers of a root of unity to form a bivariate polynomial identity, which is verified on random challenge points via the Schwartz-Zippel lemma.
- **Interactive Protocol Execution**: Each worker node maintains its own polynomials and evaluates them at a challenge point $\alpha$ received from the verifier. Evaluations are transmitted to the master node, which constructs a new polynomial identity and commits to a witness ($H_y(\alpha, Y)$). The prover cluster then evaluates this on an additional random evaluation point from the verifier and produces a bivariate KZG opening proof.
- **Arbitrary Circuit Generalization & Robustness**: Pianist extends beyond data-parallel circuits to arbitrary arithmetic circuits by implementing a distributed grand product argument. Additionally, the master node can identify faulty proof fragments from worker nodes in data-parallel setups and generate proofs for correct slices without rerunning the entire cluster.
- **Implementation & Benchmarks**: Implemented on top of the Plonk codebase in the gnark library, Pianist demonstrates that proving time and memory usage scale down proportionally as cluster size grows, maintaining low overhead even with small numbers of worker nodes.

### Takeaways
Pianist offers a fully distributed ZKP protocol for general arithmetic circuits that preserves the constant proof size, constant verification time, and quasi-linear proving computation of Plonk while requiring only $O(1)$ constant communication between the master and worker nodes, effectively removing distributed communication bottlenecks in zkRollup scaling.

talks.title: 2024 265 eAudit A Fast, Scalable and Deployable Audit Data Collection System Hanke Kimm
talks.teaser: Shows how an eBPF-based system call logger can keep up with heavy workloads while resisting attacks that erase audit records.
talks.summary:
Audit loggers are the main evidence source when investigating advanced persistent threats, because system call records preserve the links between steps of an attack. Existing collectors fall short. One widely used Linux logger slowed a benchmark workload roughly eightfold, and several measured systems dropped most events even at moderate load, with losses over 90% under heavier activity. An intruder with root access can also erase records still held in the logger's memory before they reach a secure server, a window that ranged from 50 to 500,000 records across the systems measured.

The proposed system, eAudit, captures system calls with eBPF, a safe virtual machine inside the Linux kernel that avoids changes to kernel source. A naive design that sends every event straight to user space still lost too much data. Three optimizations follow. A compact encoding reduced the average record size from about 170 bytes to about 17 bytes. Per-CPU caches batch P events before each ring buffer write. A performance model then balances overhead against latency by tuning P and the wake-up interval W, and in the experiments the optimal W was about 5 to 8.

Across benchmarks the combined optimizations brought overhead down to about 3%, a factor of 18 below the unoptimized design, and the tampering window averaged a couple hundred records. The next best system produced windows ranging from 35 to 200,000 records. The lesson for practitioners is that high-rate collectors need batching and tuned buffering, and that the size of the tampering window matters for detecting intrusions after the fact.

talks.title: 2024 431 Routing Attacks on Cryptocurrency Mining Pools Muoi Tran
talks.teaser: Shows how BGP hijacks and a Stratum V2 encryption flaw can quietly cripple cryptocurrency mining pools.
talks.summary:
Mining pools coordinate miners to build new blocks, and the speaker notes that they now produce most new blocks for many proof-of-work cryptocurrencies, with over 99% of new Bitcoin blocks coming from pools. The talk asks how a network adversary with routing control could disrupt them. Attackers could find pool server addresses, then use BGP hijacks, including origin hijacks that pass RPKI checks and sub-prefix hijacks, to pull pool-to-miner traffic through their own network.

Surveys of 55 active pools in the top ten cryptocurrencies found that 50 (91%) could be targeted. Although 93% of pool servers used RPKI, only 52% were covered by maximum-length prefix settings. Dropping every intercepted packet would be noticed quickly, so the speaker showed a stealthier route: a flaw in Stratum V2's authenticated encryption means one corrupted packet desynchronises the nonce counters. After that, the two sides cannot decrypt each other, miners keep working on stale jobs, and the symptoms look like cheating or hardware faults.

Across Bitcoin mining power, almost all autonomous systems could disrupt up to 45%, and the most powerful one could reach 96%. The vulnerability was reported to protocol developers, and a fix that resets the connection on decryption failure was merged into the main codebase in February. Short-term defences include hosting pool servers across several networks and using RPKI with maximum-length prefixes, which the speaker said would significantly reduce the number of networks able to attack at scale. The conclusion is that pools should adopt more decentralised architectures and routing-aware connections.

talks.title: 2024 467 ARMOR A Formally Verified Implementation of X 509 Certificate Chain Validation Joyanta De
talks.teaser: ARMOR presents a formally verified X.509 chain validator suited as ground truth when comparing open-source TLS certificate libraries.
talks.summary:
Public-key authentication in TLS and many other services depends on clients correctly validating X.509 certificate chains, yet implementations often diverge from RFC 5280 and have accumulated logical flaws that can undermine trust and enable man-in-the-middle attacks. Existing formally verified TLS work still treats certificate validation as a trusted black box, which motivates a dedicated, checkable implementation of chain validation itself.

The ARMOR project decomposes validation into stages—from PEM extraction and Base64 decoding through ASN.1 and X.509 parsing, name canonicalization, chain construction, and semantic checks—and specifies many components with implementation-independent relational properties proved in Agda, including soundness, completeness, and termination for a large subset of the pipeline. The talk walks through representative semantic rules, such as matching signature algorithms on a certificate and requiring CA basic constraints on issuer certificates, and notes current gaps: string canonicalization and the driver are not fully verified, and hostname checks and revocation remain future work.

Evaluation pits ARMOR against eleven open-source validators on more than four million real and synthetic chains and on browsing Alexa’s top sites via BoringSSL’s curl integration. ARMOR adheres more strictly to RFC 5280—for example on minimum name string length and critical unrecognized extensions—while incurring roughly 2.5 seconds and about 1,000 megabytes of runtime overhead versus under half a second for typical libraries. Practitioners can treat ARMOR as an open-source reference and differential test oracle, with performance optimization and end-to-end guarantees left to ongoing research.

talks.title: Backdooring Multimodal Learning
talks.teaser: A framework scores early-training samples and mixes modality triggers to poison multimodal models with fewer labeled examples.
talks.summary:
Multimodal models that fuse vision, text, and audio improve many benchmarks, yet they share the broader deep-learning risk that a data-poisoning adversary can implant triggers while leaving benign accuracy intact. Outsourced labeling amplifies that threat. Prior backdoor research focuses heavily on single-modality tasks; poisoning every modality at once often underperforms because modalities contribute unequally and interact during training.

The presenters target data- and computation-efficient poisoning. They reject late-stage forgetting scores for multimodal training and introduce an early-training BS score that weighs gradient magnitude and direction across modalities. A selection pipeline ranks clean candidates, then applies a co-attack that poisons all modalities per sample and a mix-attack that tries arbitrary modality subsets. Experiments cover visual question answering with a blue-cube image trigger and audio-video speech recognition with white-cube video and high-frequency audio triggers, under varied attacker knowledge.

Results show forgetting-based selection fails on these tasks while the proposed attacks beat random poisoning. On VQA, the question modality drives backdoor success more than the image; on AVSR, audio dominates normal accuracy but video dominates the backdoor. Partial modality poisoning can outperform poisoning everything, and small visual patches can still matter. Practitioners should treat multimodal backdoors as a distinct problem: rank poison candidates early, test per-modality triggers, and avoid assuming unimodal poisoning intuition transfers.

talks.title: Chronos presentation sard Chen
talks.teaser: Deep-priority delay fuzzing with transient timeouts finds hidden timeout bugs across ZooKeeper, HDFS, and similar distributed stacks.
talks.summary:
Distributed systems lean heavily on timeouts so nodes can retry or skip work when peers stall or messages vanish. Those mechanisms span local I/O and network paths, often spread across large codebases and runtime libraries, which makes incorrect timeout handling—timeout bugs—easy to miss and costly when they surface in production.

The presentation introduces Kronos, a testing framework built around injected delays rather than waiting for natural slowness. It instruments a system under test with fine-grained delay blocks, then drives workloads while a selector picks delay sequences using deep-priority guidance so shallow paths do not starve deeper timeout logic. A transient delay mechanism avoids wall-clock waits by forcing timeout values toward zero, keeping runs fast while still exercising real timeout handlers. An analyzer watches for crashes and hangs such as service availability breaks illustrated by an HDFS data streamer state mishandling case.

Kronos was applied to ZooKeeper, MySQL cluster, HDFS, and Go Ethereum, reporting 28 new bugs and outperforming random, brute-force, and coverage-guided fault injection baselines. A variant without transient delays found roughly half as many issues within the same time budget. Practitioners maintaining distributed platforms gain a concrete pattern for stressing timeout code paths systematically before delays in the wild trigger outages.

talks.title: MEA Defender Lv Peizhuo
talks.teaser: Explores a robust model watermark that survives black-box extraction and still verifies ownership of stolen neural networks.
talks.summary:
The presentation addresses intellectual property protection for large neural models that are costly to train and easy to copy through model extraction. An adversary with black-box query access can train a substitute model from predictions and confidence scores, which often strips conventional white-box and black-box watermarks and weakens ownership claims.

The proposed DEFender scheme embeds a watermark aligned with the main task’s input and output distributions, using an elastic backdoor-style design, combination rules on features, and verification laws so mixed or out-of-distribution probes are less likely to falsely trigger the mark. Optimization balances task utility, watermark strength, and resistance to mis-activation via multi-task learning with MGDA. Evaluations span several extraction strategies and architectures on vision and language-style tasks, reporting high watermark retention on stolen models in many settings while degraded query distributions can leave extracted models largely unusable.

Practitioners learn that watermark survivability hinges on staying in-distribution with the victim model, that extraction does not always erase marks designed this way, and that owners may still need query strategies and larger capacity when attackers hunt marks by combining samples from different labels.

talks.title: GroVE 20mins S&P Asim Waheed
talks.teaser: Explores embedding-based checks that distinguish stolen graph neural network surrogates from independently trained models.
talks.summary:
Graph neural networks power many graph-based products, yet adversaries can clone them through prediction APIs by training surrogates that match both task accuracy and behavioral fidelity. The presentation argues that surrogate and victim models produce nearly overlapping node embeddings, which makes those vectors a practical fingerprint for ownership disputes.

The proposed Grove scheme expects owners to register cryptographic commitments with secure timestamps, then lets a verifier compare suspect and claimed models via black-box APIs on a fresh sample from the same data distribution. A learned similarity classifier measures embedding distances; if enough pairs fall below a closeness threshold, the suspect is judged a copy. Experiments report zero false negatives on type-one and type-two extraction setups, with low false positives on several standard graph benchmarks, and sub-three-hour similarity-classifier training on one GPU for the largest set.

Pruning surrogates can evade naive detectors, so training augments with pruned surrogate outputs restores detection for moderate prune ratios. Double extraction weakens the attack while remaining detectable. Practitioners should treat GNN API exposure as extractable, pair registration with embedding-based verification, and harden against compression-style evasion.

talks.title: LowerBoundsRDP Tim Kutta
talks.teaser: Black-box statistical methods produce confidence intervals to audit Renyi differential privacy without algorithm source code.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that assessing privacy in practice should not rely solely on paper proofs or source inspection, and that Renyi differential privacy sits between overly strict pure DP and overly permissive approximate DP while covering mechanisms such as the Gaussian mechanism, subsampling, and shuffling. Existing black-box testers with confidence intervals target pure differential privacy and miss many algorithms that Renyi DP is meant to include.

The core contribution is estimating Renyi divergence between output distributions on adjacent databases from replicated black-box runs. Naive plug-in kernel density estimation fails when estimated densities near zero destabilize denominators; flooring helps but introduces a nondifferentiable maximum that blocks standard delta-method confidence intervals. A smoothed maximum yields an approximately normal estimator, and the paper supplies formal theory for truncation and smoothing choices.

Experiments on mechanisms including randomized response, shuffling, and the Gaussian mechanism compare simulation-based lower bounds to standardized true privacy claims. Violin plots from a thousand runs show tight lower bounds with rare overshoot, and overshoot probability stays below five percent when tuned. Practitioners gain a statistical audit tool to challenge incorrect Renyi differential privacy claims on implementations they cannot fully verify.

Detection maximizes margin over the full input space without clean samples, then ranks class scores with order-statistic p-values against a gamma null for scalability to thousand-way heads. talks.title: sokvideo v1 Max N
talks.teaser: A systematization maps explanation-aware adversarial attacks on interpretable ML systems and surveys training and inference defenses.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with an adversarial image where a classifier labels a bird as a frog while a gradient-based saliency map highlights an unrelated square, showing that attacks can target explanation outputs as well as predictions. The speakers model an explainable system as a classifier paired with an explanation method, then organize adversarial work along input manipulation, model manipulation—including data, code, and model poisoning and backdooring—and system manipulation such as fair-washing by the operator.

For explanation-aware threats they distinguish attacks that preserve explanations while changing predictions, preserve predictions while changing explanations—often to mislead fairness auditors—and dual attacks on both outputs. Within explanation-targeting settings they further separate untargeted disruption, targeted forcing of a chosen attribution pattern, and semi-targeted mappings from clean explanations. A literature survey classifies prior work by attack vector, type, and scope, noting that most studies treat one attack type and emphasize gradient-based explainers.

Defensive coverage spans training-time data validation, robust architectures and procedures, post-training checks, and inference-time input handling, monitoring, and validating explanations against predictions. The work argues that attribution robustness is an overloaded term and offers a formal hierarchy in the full paper. Practitioners should treat explanation-based assurance as bypassable when adversaries optimize for explanations, expect application-specific incentives, and treat many open questions as active research gaps.

talks.teaser: Shows a certified defense for text classifiers against word-level adversarial attacks using randomized smoothing.
talks.summary:
Language models, like image classifiers, can be fooled by small changes to their input. In text, swapping a word for a synonym, reordering words, or inserting or deleting words can flip a sentiment prediction. Earlier defenses such as adversarial training, feature detection and input transformation work only against specific attacks and can be broken by adaptive ones, so this work seeks guarantees that hold regardless of the attack.

The speaker presents Text CRS, which the authors describe as a generalized certified defense covering common word-level attacks. It applies randomized smoothing in a word embedding space and places no restrictions on model architecture. Certifying text is hard: words are discrete with no natural distance between them, insertion and deletion have no image-domain counterpart, and one sentence can contain many altered words. The method maps text into numeric embeddings, splits each attack into a permutation part and an embedding part, and uses a tailored noise distribution and certification theorem for each of the four attack types.

To improve accuracy, the authors optimize Gaussian noise per embedding dimension, add an encoder-decoder that reconstructs a cleaner embedding space, and fine-tune large models from a pretrained model trained with more noise. On synonym substitution, the framework beats the prior method at every noise level across three datasets and two models. It is the first to certify reordering, insertion and deletion, at a small accuracy cost relative to a vanilla model. Radius has a concrete meaning: 20 on a 50-word sentence allows each word to be swapped for one of its four closest synonyms, and deletion radius two allows up to two words to be removed. The code is publicly released.

talks.title: #144 TCP Spoofing Reliable Payload Transmission Past the Spoofed TCP Handshake Eric Pan
talks.teaser: Shows how spoofed TCP connections can be pushed to deliver payloads by brute-forcing windows and leaking sequence numbers.
talks.summary:
Many services trust a client's IP address for access control, such as allowlists and email sender checks. This talk studies TCP spoofing, where an attacker builds a forged connection that appears to come from a trusted address. Predicting the server's initial sequence number used to make this possible, but randomized numbers force the attacker to brute-force it by flooding the server with spoofed packets. Even after the handshake, the attacker does not know when the connection exists or which acknowledgment number to use.

The first primitive abuses acknowledgment numbers that the standard does not forbid for newly established connections, since the server has never sent data on them. Splitting the search space into window-sized pieces means that, with windows as large as 1 GB, as few as four attempts can be enough. The behavior was seen on Windows, BSD and Linux; Linux has since patched it, and the issue was reported to the IETF. The second primitive is a set of feedback channels that reveal when a spoofed handshake succeeds and what the exact acknowledgment number is. On Linux, SYN cookie sequence numbers come from a clock that updates only once per minute, so an observer can tell whether the listen backlog is full and whether a spoofed connection has cleared it. Packet reordering, loss and legitimate users add noise that reduces accuracy, which was measured in local and remote setups. Application-level channels also exist: an SMTP server's SPF check triggers DNS lookups, and a delivered email or bounce message can expose the acknowledgment number.

A measurement of the top 10,000 domains found that at least 25% of their email servers were susceptible to at least one of these feedback channels. The practical takeaway is that IP-based access control can be evaded with spoofed TCP connections, and that stricter acknowledgment validation is needed in TCP implementations.

talks.title: 699 CoreLocker Andrew Wang
talks.teaser: Extracting critical weights degrades pretrained models until authorized users restore full utility with an access key.
talks.summary:
Valuable pretrained models are costly to build and tempting targets once they ship through machine learning as a service or on-device deployment. Existing protections—watermarks, signatures, parameter encryption, and obfuscation—often break down after exposure, need extra training or data, or do not scale when many keys and versions are required.

The work presented addresses model usage control without retraining by extracting a small, significant subset of weights to act as an access key. Removing those weights degrades accuracy in a predictable way; unauthorized users interact with a weakened network, while authorized users can restore full utility. The argument rests on concentration of impact in critical weights, with theoretical bounds on how extractions propagate through layers and empirical results across convolutional, recurrent, and transformer designs. In the experiments described, performance can fall toward random-guess levels with only about two percent of weights extracted, and different extraction ratios map to different utility tiers from one base model.

For practitioners weighing how to monetize or tier access to pretrained models, the takeaway is a data-agnostic, lightweight lock that trades a controlled performance drop for recoverable full capability, backed by formal analysis rather than ad hoc obfuscation alone.

talks.title: 443 Targeted and Troublesome Zahra Moti Zahra Moti
talks.teaser: Measures trackers and targeted or inappropriate ads on websites aimed at children across Europe and North America.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a PhD student, presents a measurement study of tracking and advertising on websites aimed at children. Targeted and inappropriate ads can profile young users, and prior work suggests children misread ad messages. Because no large-scale list of child-directed sites existed, the team combined existing lists and categorization services with a multilingual machine learning classifier, followed by manual review to remove false positives.

The crawler was a heavily modified open-source tool that recorded ads, disclosure pages, third-party trackers and fingerprinting calls. It visited sites from European and North American vantage points, including a limited mobile setting, and crawled inner pages as well as homepages. An interactive step clicked the ad disclosure button to determine whether ad targeting was enabled. Across about 70,000 ads, ads appeared on 36% of sites, and on average 27% of sites showed targeted ads, a practice that regulation restricts. Over 70% of captured ads were targeted. Popular sites were more likely to switch off personalization. Improper ads in categories such as dating, weight loss, mental health and racy content appeared on 311 sites, and some sampled ad links were flagged as malicious by at least one scanner. Sites with ads triggered many trackers, with one US visit reaching 161 distinct third-party trackers.

The team contacted five companies serving racy ads, disclosed 34 such ads to Google, and shared findings with European data protection and consumer protection bodies and a UK children's digital rights group. The speaker argues for more study, rules and enforcement to safeguard children's privacy online. The source code and data are published on GitHub.

talks.title: 2024 25 MQTTactic Security Analysis and Verification for Logic Flaws in MQTT Implementations szx
talks.teaser: Explains how model checking of broker code exposed seven zero-day authorization flaws in MQTT implementations.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at whether MQTT, a publish-subscribe messaging protocol common in IoT, is secure in its broker implementations. Dozens of open-source brokers exist, and Mosquitto alone has a large deployed base, yet little prior work verified how brokers handle message delivery and authorization. Custom flows and flexible permission checks can introduce logic flaws.

The method derives a broker model from the protocol specification, covering state variables, actions and security properties. Static analysis of the source, using pointer analysis, finds the code blocks that touch state, and their execution orders become processing paths, with symbolic execution pruning infeasible ones. These paths are translated into Promela and checked with SPIN against properties such as requiring that an accepted message's sender be authorized. In Mosquitto, QoS 2 publish-release handling skipped the sender's permission check, so a malicious user could still send commands such as opening a lock to a shared device. In a separate case, a retained message let an attacker take control of a device they did not own, because permissions were checked neither on acceptance nor on delivery.

Across 27 open-source implementations, the team found seven zero-day authorization-related logic flaws. Brokers from major IoT providers, including AWS and IBM, were also affected. The takeaway is that permission checks must cover every stage of a message's lifecycle, and custom message flows need checking against the specification.

talks.title: 183 Who Left the Door Open Investigating the Causes of Exposed IoT Devices in an Academic Network
talks.teaser: Traces why campus IoT devices expose Telnet and FTP, finding manufacturers rather than owners are responsible.
talks.summary:
Researchers scanning a class B university campus, where faculty and students connect their own devices, found 220 hosts running Telnet or FTP, two risky services. Of those hosts, 185 were IoT devices. The study asked who was responsible for leaving these doors open: the device owners or the manufacturers.

The work combined several methods. A survey showed that only 2% of owners of devices with Telnet enabled by default, and 12% of owners of devices with FTP enabled by default, were aware of these services. Security notifications sent to owners produced remediation rates of 37% for Telnet and 47% for FTP, and most of the devices were confirmed as actually fixed. The most common reason for not acting was that the device did not let owners turn the services off. A review of device manuals found that many models did not describe Telnet or FTP, and most lacked security advice. A survey of manufacturers showed they knew the services existed but gave little security information about them. Penetration tests on seven IoT devices found that Telnet and FTP accepted the same default password used for the web interface, and one device allowed reading and writing of arbitrary files with root privileges.

The conclusion is that responsibility lies mainly with manufacturers rather than device owners. The practical takeaway is that fixing exposure depends on manufacturers documenting these services and providing a way to disable them.

talks.title: tor1 Zhongtang Luo
talks.teaser: Analyzes attacks on Tor's directory consensus, silent bandwidth tricks, TorEQ detection, and the Diecast hardening proposal.
talks.summary:
The talk shifts attention from Tor’s familiar three-hop relay path to the directory step clients perform first. Nine directory authorities publish signed consensus documents built from hourly votes, carrying relay views that clients treat as ground truth. The speakers describe how a malicious authority can equivocate—sending inconsistent votes to different peers—so honest authorities sign divergent consensuses while the attacker can still publish one valid-looking document and hide another, defeating Tor’s reliance on public auditing.

Empirical incidents and testnet experiments illustrate the gap between benign outages and adversarial directory members. Bandwidth inflation and sybil relay floods become harder to spot when split views block publication of conflicting documents. TorEQ adds an online detector in the Tor codebase, while Diecast reframes consensus as interactive consistency solved with parallel Byzantine broadcast, bootstrap certificates against equivocation, and compressed vote diffs to manage multi-megabyte documents under bounded synchrony.

Disclosure to the Tor project began in 2022, with the detector shipped about a year later and a Rust implementation planned as directory work continues. The closing message is that protocols weak on paper invite diverse real attacks, detection trades in new trust points, and stronger agreement machinery may be needed alongside transparency.

talks.title: 114 GAuV Xingyu Xie
talks.teaser: A graph-based verifier automates perfect semi-honest security proofs for multiparty computation protocols via simulator search.
talks.summary:
Multiparty computation protocols are often judged under simulation-based security, where proofs demand constructing a simulator whose view corrupted parties could obtain in an ideal world. Manual proof writing is tedious and error-prone, especially for perfect security without cryptographic hardness assumptions.

The presenters describe a framework that takes a protocol, builds a data-flow graph intermediate representation, and searches for a sequence of valid transformations that yield a simulator for each corrupted-party set. A worked three-party addition example shows reversing additions, wiring in the ideal functionality, and dropping redundant randomness so Charlie’s view depends only on his input and the output. They formalize valid transformations—preserving corrupted-party views and correctness—and implement two rewrite rules: equivalent rewriting and tail-node elimination. A soundness theorem links successful transformation to security, and a best-first search guided by a cost function implements the prover in a prototype called Golve.

Evaluation covers classical BGW-style arithmetic protocols and an arithmetic secret-sharing conversion protocol, with reported polynomial-time security checks for arbitrary corrupt sets on BGW when correctness holds. The approach aligns with hybrid arguments and may extend to other perfectly secure constructions. The trusted computing base is their own implementation; they do not rely on SMT solvers or mainstream proof assistants, and they point listeners to an open repository for the code.

talks.title: 431 Asterisk Super fast MPC with a Friend Protik Paul
talks.teaser: Shows an MPC protocol that reaches fairness against a malicious majority, with help from a semi-honest helper.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses secure multi-party computation, where mutually distrusting parties jointly compute a function on private inputs. The speaker explains the usual trade-off: honest-majority protocols are efficient and can offer fairness and guaranteed output delivery, but tolerate fewer corrupt parties, while dishonest-majority protocols tolerate all but one party at higher computation and communication cost. The proposed model adds a semi-honest helper party to aim for the strengths of both.

The speaker presented an impossibility result: if a malicious majority coexists with a semi-honest helper and can send non-protocol messages to it, fairness and guaranteed output delivery cannot be achieved. The construction then targets the case where either the helper is semi-honest or the majority is malicious. It relies on authenticated additive secret sharing in a pre-processing and online structure, with a common-key setup that cuts communication. Benchmarks against dishonest-majority protocols such as MCUT, MASCOT, Overdrive and assisted MPC showed large communication and throughput gains.

The dark pool application treats a regulator as the helper party, matching hidden buy and sell orders so that quantities and prices stay private until trades happen. With five parties and 500 buyers and 500 sellers in a server-outsourced setting, continuous double auction matched the requests in about 16 seconds. Volume matching with 50 buyers and 50 sellers, all taking part in the computation, finished in under two minutes. The talk closes by noting that achieving guaranteed output delivery without a helper remains open, and that the framework could extend to privacy-preserving machine learning and federated learning.

talks.title: gpuzip 20 yingchen wang
talks.teaser: GPU graphical data compression leaks compressibility through microarchitecture traces, enabling collocated pixel-stealing in browsers.
talks.summary:
The presentation revisits compression side channels from CRIME and related TLS attacks, where compressibility reveals secrets when attacker-controlled data is mixed with user data. It argues that conventional mitigations assume compression is software-visible and documented. Graphical data compression on modern GPUs is different: vendors embed it in the microarchitecture to cut memory bandwidth as resolutions and refresh rates climb, often expanding on-chip storage while using auxiliary surfaces to mark which tile blocks compressed.

The work reverse engineers vendor-specific schemes—including Intel integrated GPU tiling and AMD delta color compression—and introduces tooling to dump, decode, and interact with compressed surfaces. A leakage model shows compressible versus incompressible patterns leave distinguishable traces in the memory controller and last-level cache, observable via DRAM traffic counters or rendering time. The talk ties this to pixel-stealing: after browsers moved SVG filters to constant-time GPU paths, compressibility of black versus turbulent surfaces still differentiates timing, letting collocated JavaScript recover cross-origin iframe pixels one at a time. An end-to-end demo extracts a Wikipedia username from a phishing scenario using only rendering time.

Practitioners should treat everything drawn on screen as potentially secret-dependent on the GPU and assume no software knob to disable hardware compression today. Mitigations discussed include vendor-exposed disable controls, Mesa patches to create textures without compression, and broader need for a hardware–software contract; the patch is framed as a partial workaround with performance cost.

talks.title: 239 Nebula A Privacy First Platform for Data Backhaul Jean Luc Watson
talks.teaser: Shows how passing phones can relay battery sensor data while the platform cannot learn who sent what.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Nebula, a backhaul system for battery-powered sensors spread across cities, forests and shipped packages. Common options are hard to scale or costly: manual retrieval, ad hoc Wi-Fi, and power-hungry cellular radios. Newer designs let nearby devices such as phones relay sensor data, but services like Amazon Sidewalk and Apple's Find My let the provider see all relay traffic, which can reveal where mule owners go. Academic metadata-hiding schemes protect privacy but struggle at the scale of millions of devices.

Nebula routes payloads directly from mules to application servers, bypassing the provider. Applications pre-purchase unlinkable Privacy Pass tokens each epoch, and a mule earns one token per delivered payload. The provider learns only aggregate token and upload counts. Sensors sign their payloads so servers can reject invalid ones, and servers commit to a token before receiving data. If a server returns a bad or spent token, the mule files a rate-limited complaint at epoch end; if it has no token, it can resubmit the payload through the provider. Duplicate complaints are resolved first come, first served.

Bluetooth sampling in a park suggested a mule every few minutes lasting 5 to 10 seconds, enough to move roughly 2 to 16 kilobytes. A single 128-core server processed about 445,000 tokens per second and over 240 million tokens per dollar. The takeaway is that metered backhaul can be offered while keeping metadata private, with energy and memory models left in the paper.

talks.title: 582 Janus Safe Biometric Deduplication for Humanitarian Aid Distribution kasra EdalatNejad
talks.teaser: Privacy-preserving deduplication lets aid groups detect repeat registrants via biometrics without risky central databases.
talks.summary:
Humanitarian distributors must block people from registering twice for limited aid without relying on phones or government IDs that fail in conflict zones. Biometrics work for deduplication, but storing templates on vulnerable populations creates grave risks if devices or databases fall into hostile hands.

The Janus design answers whether deduplication can run with only a binary new-or-duplicate outcome. Requirements span low false rejects for eligible people, no leakage beyond membership status, resilience to passive and active compromise including captured hardware, and scale to roughly ten thousand users. Trust splits between the registration station and a biometric provider; workflows delete plaintext and raw biometrics after each decision. Three builds use secure multiparty computation, a hybrid of homomorphic encryption with garbled circuits and secret sharing, and trusted hardware. The hybrid path encrypts templates, computes matching distances on ciphertext, and compares thresholds without exposing sensitive distances.

Practitioners should treat fusion across multiple fingers or irises as essential: single-sample error rates explode at ten-thousand scale, while four samples restore practicality. Reported hybrid Janus costs for eight thousand users with four fingers land near four seconds of computation and about 150 megabytes of transfer.

talks.title: 270 An Analysis of Recent Advances in Deepfake Image Detection in an Evolving Threat Landscape sif
talks.teaser: Shows that deepfake image detectors generalize poorly and can be evaded with semantic edits, then tests ways to harden them.
talks.summary:
Synthetic images from generative models such as GANs and Stable Diffusion can now be made from a text prompt, and they can power fake social accounts, fabricated news imagery and identity spoofing. This research asks whether eight state-of-the-art supervised deepfake image detectors are robust enough for that threat. The analysis is organized around three requirements: sound training and evaluation, generalization to new generators, and resilience to adversarial attacks.

On training practice, the speaker shows that a detector that scores very highly on a dataset with uncontrolled content and low-quality fakes drops sharply when content and quality are controlled, falling to 49% accuracy. The team then fine-tuned all eight detectors on a higher-quality dataset for fair evaluation. For generalization, they tested detectors against user-customized Stable Diffusion LoRA models, where most detectors lost a large share of fake-image recall, and the best single detector still averaged 19.6% degradation. Ensembling a foundation-model detector with a frequency-based one cut average degradation to 8%, and adding noise-residual frequency features improved a frequency detector's average from 19.7% to 16.7%.

For adversarial robustness, the researchers showed that careful semantic edits, such as adding lipstick through a StyleCLIP-based generator, can fool a detector without adding visible noise, using a black-box surrogate classifier. Generating over 800 such images cost about $10 on an A100 GPU. A larger foundation model in the defense reduced degradation to about 1%, and adversarial training helped the most robust detectors, though the speaker cautioned that attackers can adapt. The takeaway for practitioners is to evaluate detectors on diverse content, across unseen generators and under adversarial attack.

talks.title: cut final presentation Sönke Huster
talks.teaser: A virtio-backed fuzzer runs Linux Wi-Fi and Bluetooth stacks in QEMU and finds remotely reachable kernel bugs, including beacon-frame flaws.
talks.summary:
Wireless interfaces in the Linux kernel parse complex, attacker-influenced frames, yet earlier fuzzing often missed deep or realistic paths in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth subsystems. The work targets that gap with a dedicated fuzzer wired through a universal virtio device in QEMU, so the guest believes it has ordinary network hardware while inputs and virtio queues are tunneled to the fuzzer over Unix sockets.

Three design themes shape the tool: reach deeper kernel areas than prior efforts, seed runs with authentic traffic collected via a proxy to real controllers, and add new targets through small JSON virtio configs plus lightweight KCOV annotation patches. Coverage uses shared-memory KCOV (bitmap and comparison tracking), libAFL building blocks, and crash detection via the kernel log. Evaluation over 24 hours shows higher basic-block coverage than syzkaller on the same targets, with real-world seeds giving a multi-hour head start.

Reported outcomes include 31 new vulnerabilities and six CVEs, split across Bluetooth and Wi-Fi stacks, spanning heap overflows, use-after-free, null dereferences, out-of-bounds access, leaks, and infinite loops. Several Wi-Fi issues lie in passively received beacon handling, enabling denial of service and potentially remote code execution without tricking users onto a rogue access point; some findings trace back to kernels as old as 5.1 for Wi-Fi and 2.6.2 for Bluetooth. Practitioners can reuse the GPLv3 code to fuzz additional virtio-described devices with minimal integration work.

talks.title: Ati Priya Bajaj Len or index or count, anything but v1 Predicting Variable Names in Decompilation Ou
talks.teaser: Presents a model that suggests meaningful variable names for decompiled functions, trained via source code transfer learning.
talks.summary:
Decompilers replace variable names with placeholders such as A1 or V2, which hides what each variable means and slows reverse engineering. In tests of existing name predictors, one of the most frequent outputs was the uninformative name V2. This talk presents VarBERT, a model that predicts a meaningful name for each variable and whether the variable is human-created or an extraneous artifact added by a compiler or decompiler.

VarBERT is pretrained with masked language modeling on source code, which is easier to collect at scale, then fine-tuned on decompiled functions from IDA and Ghidra. Its dataset, VarCorpus, draws on 112,000 C and C++ libraries and executables built at four optimization levels, O0 through O3, with 2.6 million unique functions. Three problems were handled along the way: extraneous variables are labelled rather than mapped to a developer name, debug type information is replaced with generic scalar types so debug and stripped output look alike, and duplicate functions from repository forks and shared utilities are removed by normalizing and hashing function bodies. VarBERT reached 50% accuracy, which the speaker reported as 12% above one existing approach and 14% above DIRE. Pretraining lifted accuracy from 39% to 54% in an ablation, and training on only 20% of the data still gave 41% name accuracy and 77% origin accuracy.

A model trained on a separate set of non-x86-64 binaries reached 46% in IDA and 50% in Ghidra. A case study showed that exact-match scoring may be too strict, since a prediction that carries the same meaning as the original name still counts as a miss. The speaker closed by noting that the datasets, models and code are open source, so decompiler users can run the models to get name suggestions.

talks.title: CanWeCastABallotAsIntendedAndBeReceiptFree Henri Devillez
talks.teaser: Explores when e-voting can combine cast-as-intended assurance with receipt-freeness across interactive ballot submission models.
talks.summary:
The presentation examines electronic voting architectures where voters interact with devices and casting servers, after which ballots and proofs appear on a public bulletin board and talliers publish verified results. It separates verifiability goals—ensuring recorded ballots match what voters intended and explain the final tally—from privacy goals, including receipt-freeness, where voters cannot hand third parties cryptographic evidence of their choices.

The work formalizes receipt-freeness when adversaries supply adaptive, multi-message instructions and may demand execution transcripts. A central negative result shows cast-as-intended and receipt-freeness cannot both hold if ballot submission is entirely non-interactive; the argument couples receipt-freeness, deceiving correctness, and cast-as-intended games via parallel adversaries. On the constructive side, three protocols reconcile the properties by allowing interaction during submission or during earlier registration, using tools such as encrypted vote shares, randomized ciphertexts, voter-held commitment randomness, and divertible zero-knowledge proofs.

Practitioners building verifiable yet coercition-resistant voting systems should treat interaction as structurally necessary rather than optional, and weigh voter workload against round complexity when selecting among the human-oriented multi-round design, the fixed three-round variant, or the pre-registration alternative with heavier cryptography.

talks.title: 2024 108 DeepShuffle A Lightweight Defense Framework against Adversarial Fault Injection Attacks on
talks.teaser: Shows how DeepShuffle moves the target of voltage-based fault attacks on neural network accelerators in shared FPGA clouds.
talks.summary:
The talk covers fault injection against deep neural network accelerators on FPGAs shared in multi-tenant cloud servers. Because the programmable chip shares resources such as the power distribution network, one tenant's circuits can indirectly disturb another's computation. It recaps DeepDup, an earlier attack that uses supply voltage fluctuations to inject well-timed faults that degrade inference. The work asks whether DeepDup also affects a highly optimized open-source accelerator, TVM VTA, and whether a lightweight mitigation exists.

The reproduced attack did less damage to TVM VTA than to hand-built accelerators, mainly because its first convolutional layer and final fully connected layer run on an ARM core outside the FPGA. The proposed DeepShuffle defense changes the order of weight transmission on each inference, a moving-target approach. Permuting a convolutional layer's output channels shuffles its feature maps, and applying the same permutation to the connected layer keeps the computation correct with no extra operators. Across five accelerators and two datasets, DeepShuffle forced the attacker to need more rounds, and a targeted attack still left the chosen class detectable after 1,000 rounds.

Layer analysis on ResNet-20 found the fourth, seventh and last layers especially vulnerable, reaching random-guess accuracy in 30 attack rounds, and DeepShuffle improved them, though weaknesses remained. Future work could redesign those layers or move their workload to the CPU. Takeaways: the defense randomizes the attacker's best opportunities, needs no retraining, and is argued to apply beyond vision models.

talks.title: 588 From Principle to Practice Vertical Data Minimization for Machine Learning Robin Staab
talks.teaser: Explains how coarsening personal attributes cuts data collected for machine learning, with a privacy-aware tree method.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces vertical data minimization, which reduces the personal data collected for machine learning inference by replacing each original attribute value with a coarser generalized value. The speaker ties this to data minimization rules in European and US policy, which target what an untrusted collector gathers. Unlike horizontal minimization, which drops records and suits training but not inference, this keeps every record while coarsening its fields. On an employment dataset, unique field values fall from 196 to 34 while downstream accuracy drops by about 1%.

The authors ask how such generalizations can be learned and how they should be judged. They require generalizations to be global, applied per attribute, and strictly partitioning. Baselines include uniform range splitting, feature selection and an earlier tree-pruning method. Their main approach, a privacy-aware decision tree, adds a privacy term to the usual splitting criterion, with a parameter that trades privacy against utility, and the tree's decision boundaries define the generalization. For evaluation they define eight adversary scenarios aligned with regulator guidance, covering reconstruction, linkage and singling out.

Across datasets, this method gave the best privacy-utility tradeoff, keeping utility close to unminimized data while sacrificing little privacy against reconstruction. It also stayed stable under distribution shifts. The takeaway for practitioners is that minimizing data at collection can complement other privacy technologies, since it changes what is collected rather than how.

talks.title: 433 On SMS Phishing Tactics and Infrastructure Alex Nahapetyan
talks.teaser: Traces SMS phishing campaigns from public gateways, revealing hosting, certificate timing and suspected delivery-route tests.
talks.summary:
SMS phishing lures victims to web pages that collect personal or financial details, and the researchers treat it as both a telecom abuse and a web abuse problem. To gather samples, they crawled eleven public SMS gateway websites, which show messages sent to a number and earn money from ads. They collected over 200 million messages, flagged about 60,000 as phishing using VirusTotal with an engine threshold, grouped them into roughly 35,000 campaigns, and linked those into more than 600 operations.

Most links redirected to a different host than the one shown in the text, and most certificates were issued weeks before the message was seen. Cloudflare, AWS and Google were common hosts, and no seasonal pattern appeared. Top second-level domains looked like URL shorteners, but only two were public services. Some campaigns had a route label followed by a number, and 16 host names had certificates issued 12 hours after the first message, pointing to delivery tests before real sends. Most operations (87%) named no detectable entity; the ones that did mentioned brands such as Apple and the Australian government.

Operations were short-lived, used one or two URLs, and targeted English speakers in the United States, UK and Canada. They also found over 40,000 LinkedIn posts advertising bulk SMS services, some promoted in Telegram groups. Their main lesson is that gateways can reveal campaigns before victims receive them, and that bulk messaging interfaces are an access control issue.

talks.title: 574 Cohere Managing Differential Privacy in Large Scale Systems Nicolas Küchler
talks.teaser: Shows how a shared privacy budget can be tracked and allocated across differential privacy applications in a large system.
talks.summary:
Differential privacy lets organizations share statistics about a population while limiting what can be learned about any single person. The talk argues that existing differential privacy frameworks give guarantees only per application, so when several applications touch the same users, the real cumulative privacy loss can be underestimated. To address this, the speaker presents Cohere, a system that tracks one shared privacy state across applications built by different teams and in different libraries.

The design has several parts. Noise mechanisms from each framework are intercepted and analyzed jointly, enabling tighter Rényi differential privacy composition than epsilon-delta composition. Partitioning attributes such as country define hypothetical user blocks so that applications touching different subsets are tracked finely, and subsampling reduces cost when only part of the population is needed. To keep budgets renewable, users are retired once their consumption reaches a threshold and replaced by new users, instead of periodically refreshing budgets for everyone.

In the evaluation, the system was compared with PrivateCube, a Kubernetes extension for privacy resources, over simulated weekly allocations spanning 40 weeks. On mixed machine learning and analytics workloads, it achieved a 1.5x improvement in accepted requests over a first-come, first-served baseline, rising to 9x when a utility metric reflecting application priority was optimized. The takeaway is that fine-grained privacy accounting and priority-aware allocation matter for shared systems.

talks.title: 02 Saiid El Hajj Chehade SINBAD 20 min Saiid El Hajj Chehade
talks.teaser: An ML pipeline flags ad-blocker breakage by section, simulating clicks to catch dynamic failures filter list updates cause.
talks.summary:
Ad blockers and similar privacy tools often break websites when filter lists change, leaving users unable to use expected page functionality. Maintainers today rely on slow user reports and manual reproduction, and prior automated checks either miss interaction-dependent dynamic breakage or suffer high false positives from coarse heuristics and noisy training labels.

The presentation introduces Sinbad, a three-stage automated pipeline that crawls each page with fixed, broken, and unfiltered list versions, segments content semantically, ranks salient regions, and performs targeted interactions before comparing DOM trees into labeled edit subtrees. Features span visual, functional, and page-context signals; a subtree classifier trained on hundreds of manually verified AdGuard issues reaches strong cross-validated discrimination, and page-level decisions aggregate broken subtrees with fewer false positives than earlier heuristic and graph-based baselines.

Practitioners learn that breakage is partly subjective and that roughly a quarter of reported cases are dynamic, so scalable detection must model where users care and what they click. Sinbad is modular for better segmentation or saliency components, though custom filter lists, fast-changing sites, unsupported cookie banners, and randomized page content remain practical limits.

talks.title: 272 SneakyPrompt Jailbreaking Text to image Generative Models Yuchen Yang
talks.teaser: Presents an automated reinforcement-learning method that finds adversarial prompts bypassing text-to-image safety filters.
talks.summary:
Text-to-image generators such as Stable Diffusion and DALL-E 2 are usually paired with safety filters that block sexually explicit or violent outputs. The talk explains that these filters can act on the text embedding, on the generated image, or on both. Attackers have relied on handcrafted prompts, which rarely succeed, or on optimization methods that need very many queries, each of which carries a cost.

The speaker presents SneakyPrompt, an automatic search that uses reinforcement learning to swap sensitive words in a target prompt for nonsensical or harmless-looking tokens. A shadow text encoder supplies the semantic reference, the reward is the similarity between that reference and the image produced, and each extra query adds a penalty. Across six open-source filters on Stable Diffusion, the attack achieved a high one-time bypass rate using about 40 queries on average. Against the closed-box filter of DALL-E 2, it reached a 57 percent one-time bypass rate with roughly 24 queries, which the speaker described as the first such bypass using real sensitive images. Ablations showed that matching the shadow encoder to the target improves image quality, and that the cosine-similarity reward yields higher bypass rates. Stricter similarity thresholds and larger search spaces trade bypass rate against query count.

The main takeaway is that filters relying on text or image matching can be evaded by prompts that look benign to a human reviewer. The findings were disclosed to OpenAI and Stability AI, and the tool and data were released publicly.

talks.title: 308 SoK CollusionResistantMPSI Jelle Vos
talks.teaser: Systematizes multi-party private set intersection protocols, compares their costs, and flags common design pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The talk covers multi-party private set intersection (MPSI), where several parties each hold a set and only the common elements are revealed, to a designated leader. The focus is on collusion-resistant variants, which stay secure even when a set number of participants work together. The research systematizes existing protocols into three high-level constructions: private homomorphic set representations, leaky ones that need secure computation before anything is revealed, and aggregatable membership queries. Four set encodings are walked through as examples: bit sets, Bloom filters, single-hash sets and polynomial roots.

To compare protocols fairly, the authors instantiated several published designs with the same additively homomorphic encryption scheme and counted elliptic curve multiplications. The results show that no protocol is best in every setting, and that the outcome depends on parameters such as thread count, CPU and network latency. Many recent papers also ignore older insights that still apply. Common pitfalls include releasing a Bloom filter without querying it under encryption, which leaks information about the input sets, and using unsafe randomness, such as leader-supplied randomness that colluding parties can undo. Adapting protocols to the malicious model adds further fragile points.

The main takeaways are that real-world parameters for MPSI protocols are still unknown, that older insights remain relevant, and that protocol descriptions should be written at a general level using reusable primitives such as oblivious key-value stores and encrypted membership query filters.

talks.title: 79 Leaky Address Masking Mathé Hertogh 1
talks.teaser: Shows how unmasked Spectre gadgets and linear address masking enable arbitrary kernel data leakage on Intel, AMD, and Arm CPUs.
talks.summary:
The presentation revisits Spectre-style disclosure gadgets after years of kernel hardening against classic double-array indexing patterns. While masked gadgets were cataloged and mitigated, pointer-chasing code that doubly dereferences pointers was widely dismissed as non-exploitable. A kernel scan finds more than 16,000 such unmasked gadgets in Linux, dwarfing earlier masked-gadget counts.

The core challenge is leaking through unmasked 64-bit pointer chasing: canonical address rules, SMAP, and cache entropy block naive data-cache channels. The approach chains three ideas—using linear address masking (and analogous Arm and AMD features) so ASCII secrets satisfy reduced canonical checks, abusing translation-before-SMAP ordering to leak via the TLB instead of the data cache, and mapping 128 user pages per byte to brute-force the remaining entropy when partial plaintext is known.

The resulting SLAM Spectre attack recovers sensitive files such as shadow password hashes from current Linux within minutes across multiple exploited gadgets. Mitigation discussion covers vendor responses, including earlier SMAP enforcement and coordination with kernel guidance before future silicon ships.

talks.title: 243 MAWSEO Adversarial Wiki Search Poisoning for Illicit Online Promotion Zilong Lin
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers can poison MediaWiki search rankings and slip promotional edits past vandalism detectors.
talks.summary:
Illicit promotion, such as advertising illegal online pharmacies, has long relied on black hat SEO on compromised pages. This talk asks whether wiki systems can be abused in the same way, boosting promoted content in search results while avoiding vandalism detection and reader suspicion. The attacker has to meet four goals at once: insert promotional text in wiki style, raise the article's search rank, evade a black-box vandalism detector, and keep the edit semantically consistent and relevant to its topic.

The proposed approach, called MAWSEO, works in five steps. It fetches a target article, generates candidate promotional paragraphs with an injection model, retrieves the best candidate using a multitask adversarial retrieval model with a discriminator for each objective, picks an insertion point by semantic similarity to neighbouring paragraphs, and inserts the paragraph. Substitute ranking and vandalism models are trained by querying a search API and the ORES API. In experiments on a local MediaWiki copy of 123,000 articles, promoting 125 illicit online pharmacies across 659 query terms, it outperformed keyword stuffing and other adversarial ranking baselines. A user study with 104 valid responses found the revised articles seemed trustworthy.

On the defense side, the speaker described a coherence detector that scores the joints between sentences, which was more effective than adversarial training with generated revisions, and the two were presented as complementary. The talk also compared ChatGPT, which was weaker at rank boosting and evasion, and reported similar results for illicit online casino promotion. The takeaway is that wiki search and vandalism tooling need coherence checks alongside traditional moderation.

talks.title: 556 Pudding Private User Discovery in Anonymity Networks Ceren Kocaogullar
talks.teaser: Explains a way for users of anonymity networks to find each other by email address without leaking who searches for whom.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a gap in anonymity networks: they hide who is talking to whom, but they offer no usable way for people to find each other. Messaging apps made end-to-end encryption routine, yet users of systems like Loopix still have to pass around public keys or network addresses. The speaker argues that email addresses work well as usernames because they are readable and already sit in phone contact books. The naive approach of a discovery server fails in two ways. A malicious server learns that a searcher is looking for a particular person, and it can hand back a key that does not belong to that person. A malicious user can also probe arbitrary usernames to learn which ones are registered.

The proposed system, called Pudding, is an application layer built on Loopix that needs no changes to the network. It runs several discovery nodes, with 3f+1 nodes tolerating up to f faulty ones. Lookups use a deterministic single-use reply block, seeded from a hash of the email address and a secret shared among the nodes, so every node produces the same values. The discovery nodes blind the target's public key and reflect the searcher's message to the target, who can unblind it. For unregistered names, the nodes return random-looking fake values, so a searcher cannot tell whether a user exists. Long-term contacts are set up with a modified Sigma key exchange that supports blinded signatures. Registration is optional and uses a single email reply, checked with DKIM signatures and node challenges, with a threshold of 2f+1 confirmations.

The speaker maps the design back to four goals: unlinkability, resistance to impersonation, external identity verification and membership unobservability. The system was implemented on the Nym network. Reported average latencies for the one-time operations stayed under 13 seconds, and the speaker notes that throughput limits of the underlying network dominate performance.

talks.title: 526 From Virtual Touch to Tesla Command Unlocking Unauthenticated Control Chains From Smart Glasses
talks.teaser: Attackers can chain electromagnetic touch spoofing on smart glasses with mobile automation to issue unauthenticated Tesla commands.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how consumer gadgets link into longer control paths where trust passes from device to device without users noticing. A smart glass pairs to a phone authorized for Tesla, and the owner issues car commands through a voice assistant on the glasses. The team asks whether weak points let an outsider start the chain and steer the vehicle without the owner’s interaction or normal authentication.

They study capacitive touch on commercial smart glasses, inspired by prior work on strong electromagnetic interference mimicking force touch. They sweep roughly 100 MHz to 1 GHz, tear down sample hardware, model charge-time capacitance sensing on a prototype, and build a higher-intensity oscillator to reach useful range. EMI can wake the voice assistant while the phone stays locked. They then chain platform automation—Shortcuts on iPhone and similar flows on Android through third-party Tesla tooling—so spoken commands reach Tesla APIs. Indoor tests across several glasses models report near-perfect success; outdoor scenarios near coffee shops, chargers, and parking areas show roughly seven-second attacks with inexpensive gear, with voice commands tuned for reliability under ambient noise.

Practitioners should treat each new link in a voice-and-automation chain as transitive trust: shielding touch sensors is hard, so phone and app designers need stricter integration testing and risk review for third parties. The speakers suggest anomaly checks—such as unlock requests when the user is far from the car—and passive presence cues on glasses (skin, airflow, IMU liveness, synthetic-voice discrimination) as directions for mitigation without breaking accessibility for routine use.

talks.title: 2024 500 Exploring the Orthogonality and Linearity of Backdoor Attacks Kaiyuan Zhang
talks.teaser: Explains why some neural network backdoors survive later training and why certain defenses fail, using orthogonality and linearity.
talks.summary:
The talk examines backdoor attacks on machine learning models, where a hidden trigger changes model behaviour while the model otherwise performs normally. The speaker notes that existing defenses do not always succeed, and asks what makes some defenses fail against particular attacks. The work frames backdoor learning as a two-task continual learning problem: the backdoor is picked up quickly in an early phase, while the clean task is learned more gradually afterward.

Using a theoretical argument, the research proves that a backdoor learned in the first stage remains unaffected by gradient descent during a second, clean training stage. The author introduces two metrics. Orthogonality is measured as the angle between backdoor and clean gradients, and linearity is measured by fitting a linear regression across network layers. Across 14 attacks and 12 defenses, patch and blend attacks show higher orthogonality and linearity, while filter, invisible and composite attacks score lower. Pruning and unlearning-based defenses are described as working better when the separation between backdoor and clean behaviour is strong, while weight-based and trigger-inversion defenses vary with the degree of linearity.

The main takeaway is that these metrics can help predict when a given defense will succeed or fail. The speaker encourages researchers to report them alongside attack success rate and accuracy when evaluating new defenses and attacks.

talks.title: 2024 614 Few shot Unlearning Youngsik Yoon
talks.teaser: Presents a few-shot machine unlearning method that removes, protects or corrects target data when only a few samples are available.
talks.summary:
Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of a specific subset of training data from a trained model, such as data that is mislabeled, sensitive, or otherwise unwanted. Retraining from scratch without that data is the straightforward option, but it is costly, and earlier methods usually need the full original training set to approximate it. This talk addresses the harder case where only a few target samples are available and the remaining affected examples are unspecified.

The proposed framework has three steps. First, model inversion synthesizes images from the trained model, guided by the few target samples and a general data-domain prior. Second, filtration discards low-confidence images and keeps those close to the target samples in embedding space. Third, an unlearning step applies a strategy matched to the goal: removal, privacy protection, or label correction.

Three scenarios were evaluated. In class removal, accuracy on the erased class dropped near zero while other classes stayed accurate. For privacy protection, the privacy-oriented variants lowered membership inference success compared with standard unlearning while keeping accuracy. For correcting mislabeled crossed sevens, a clear gap between correction and plain removal showed that erasing alone does not fix the wrong behavior. The takeaway: few-shot unlearning can work from very limited samples, and the goal should shape the update.
