talks.title: ItsSimplexIEEES+P 20min Andrew Cullen
talks.teaser: Tighter smoothing certificates, expectation-sharing ensembles, and a two-class simplex view explain certified-robustness gains.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on adversarial examples that flip classifier predictions while staying close to benign inputs, and on why pointwise defenses lack general guarantees. It motivates certified robustness: bounds stating that no adversarial point lies within a finite radius, supporting detection prioritization and risk ranking of samples.

The core contribution revisits randomized smoothing, where Gaussian-noisy copies of an input are classified many times to estimate expectations. Building on tighter differential-privacy analysis for Gaussian mechanisms, the authors derive improved certificates that uniformly strengthen earlier Lecuyer-style softmax and argmax certifications and compare favorably to Lee and Cohen on standard certified-accuracy curves. They show multiple certificates built from the same expectations can be combined by taking the maximum radius at negligible extra cost, yielding an ensemble that dominates individual methods on median certified radius and coverage. The Simplex of possible outputs visualizes the top two class expectations to explain when each technique wins and how ImageNet outputs on ResNet populate regions dominated by Cohen, Lee, or the new method.

Practitioners should treat certification as a toolkit rather than a single formula: reuse expensive sampling across schemes, ensemble for best-in-class radii, and use the simplex view to interpret dataset, model, and training effects on certified performance.

talks.title: 428 Understanding the Privacy Practices of Political Campaigns A Perspective from the 2020 US Electi
talks.teaser: Measures how US election campaign websites collect voter data and whether their privacy policies disclose it.
talks.summary:
This talk examines privacy practices on the websites of US election campaigns, using the 2020 cycle as its basis. Political campaigns gather large amounts of personal data, yet they are generally outside US privacy regulation because they are treated as nonprofits. The research focused on websites because campaigns use them to collect data at scale and to direct voters toward signing up, donating or volunteering.

The team built a pipeline that found candidates' campaign sites through a political encyclopedia, crawled them, pulled out privacy policy text and analyzed it. Across more than 2,000 House, Senate and presidential campaign sites, about 71% collected personal data, using 28 distinct data types. Some campaigns also gathered details about parents, friends or partners, and about 3% collected socioeconomic opinions. Among campaigns that had a policy, 41% did not disclose all of the data they collected, compared with 25% of smart home vendors in earlier work. None of the campaigns described what happens to collected data after the election ends. In a test where the researchers signed up for 26 campaigns, eight shared the test email addresses with others, three of them without telling the tester.

Campaign responses pointed to a misunderstanding of what privacy policies are, limited technical staff and the absence of federal law. The speaker concludes that targeted regulation and clear, accessible disclosure are needed so voters can make informed choices about their data.

talks.title: 354 Tabbed Out Subverting the Android Custom Tab Security Model Philipp Beer
talks.teaser: Shows how a potentially unwanted Android app can abuse Custom Tabs to infer user state, leak URLs and fake websites.
talks.summary:
Android apps can open web pages in Custom Tabs, which run in the user's browser and share its cookies and state, while still reporting navigation events back to the launching app. The authors asked whether this model is truly secure. They combined a review of official documentation, reading Chrome's source code, manual API testing, and comparison with web standards. This produced six vulnerabilities, reported to browser vendors, which led to three CVEs.

Three of the attacks belong to a new class the authors call cross-context leaks. The state inference attack hides a custom tab behind another screen and reads callbacks such as navigation started, finished, failed and aborted, along with redirects, status codes, content types and load timing, to guess whether a user is logged in on a site. The bottom bar leak abuses the intent fired when the user taps the bar, which carries the page URL; a fake cookie banner can lure a tap that exposes a URL that may identify the user. A separate phishing attack uses the bar's trusted look to show a fake account warning that leads to a credential-harvesting page.

Many cross-site leak defences, such as frame ancestors and X-Frame-Options, do not apply because custom tab navigations count as top-level. Some cookie and fetch metadata weaknesses were fixed after reports. The talk proposed letting servers detect custom tab requests and redirect them to the default browser, and restricting state sharing unless users grant permission. Google fixed implementation issues but treats the state inference and bottom bar phishing attacks as working as intended.

talks.title: 362 Thwarting Last Minute Voter Coercion Rosario Giustolisi
talks.teaser: A cryptographic internet-voting design blends dynamic credentials with deniable revoting to defeat last-minute coercion.
talks.summary:
Internet-based voting promises convenience but must preserve privacy and resist coercion: an observer should not learn how someone voted even when watching them cast a ballot. Established schemes use fake credentials or deniable revoting, yet revoting alone cannot stop coercion in the final moments before submission, and fake credentials rely on trusted registration and special devices.

The presentation introduces dynamic credentials that evolve with voting behavior, combined with deniable revoting and server-generated noise ballots indistinguishable from voter ballots. Each voter’s cast-ballot record on a bulletin board accumulates ballots; encrypted index lists let the voter and server alone distinguish coerced from genuine casts, so the server can randomize or cancel coerced choices. Walkthroughs cover revoting under initial coercion, failed coercion when the voter changes mind, and abstention. Index values update via a compact binary encoding; ballots use ElGamal-style ciphertexts, and the server proves correct handling with a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof without being fully trusted.

Coercion resistance is quantified: a coercer guessing index lists faces combinatorial growth in the number of ballots, while noticeable abuse can be throttled. A Python prototype reports sub-10 millisecond ballot generation and tallying for about one million voters in under a minute on a laptop. Practitioners gain a concrete pattern for last-minute coercion resistance without sacrificing efficient tallying from deniable revoting alone.

talks.title: 174 Automated Synthesis of Effect Graph Policies for Microservice Aware Stateful System Call Special
talks.teaser: Shows how automatically built effect graphs can limit containerized microservices to the system calls their configuration needs.
talks.summary:
This talk presents a way to lock down microservices running in containers on large cloud platforms. A compromised container could reach the host kernel and affect other customers. Existing syscall restriction policies are often stateless allow lists, so an attacker can stay within the list and still cause harm, a mimicry attack. A web server, for example, may carry an execve call it never needs when configured only to serve static files.

The proposed technique, micro execution, combines static analysis with lightweight dynamic tracing to build an effect graph for each microservice. Static analysis alone can overapproximate behavior because indirect jumps and configuration inputs are hard to resolve, while tracing alone struggles to link observed calls to program locations. Effect graph nodes are system call sites annotated with concrete arguments, and edges capture the calls made there. At runtime, a monitor treats the graph as an automaton and raises an alert when an observed call cannot advance it, such as an Engine X web server connecting to an external command-and-control server.

Evaluation reported good coverage of effectful terms and graph sizes that did not grow much as binaries grew. A proxy web server handling a million requests showed manageable resource use, and monitors used up to two cores and under 50 megabytes of RAM per node. In a hotel reservation architecture, a compromised search microservice that reached a MongoDB database directly was flagged. The main takeaway is that configuration-specific, stateful policies can be synthesized automatically and enforced across whole microservice architectures.

talks.title: 155 Specular Towards Secure, Trust minimized Optimistic Blockchain Execution Zhe Ye
talks.teaser: Shows how a rollup dispute protocol can verify any EVM client by checking a single abstract instruction on chain.
talks.summary:
Optimistic rollups let users submit blockchain transactions that an off-chain executor runs, and anyone can challenge a wrong result. Re-running the full EVM on chain to settle a challenge is too expensive, so interactive fraud proofs narrow the dispute to one step. Current designs compile an EVM client into a reduced instruction set such as MIPS and commit to that binary on chain, which ties the system to one implementation and enlarges the trusted base.

The proposed system, Specular, moves the on-chain referee to a layer of EVM semantics instead of a specific binary. The referee emulates one EVM instruction at a time, with state kept in authenticated structures such as a hash chain for the stack and a Merkle tree for memory. Any EVM implementation that follows those semantics can join a challenge, so the trusted base is just the referee and client upgrades need no on-chain change.

The authors added minimal changes to Go Ethereum and a second popular client, then tested random transactions against Uniswap, the Ethereum Name Service and a ballot contract, with dispute resolution performance described as practical. The speaker argues that targeting the highest semantic level suits remote computation beyond rollups. The takeaway is a permissionless, trustless interactive fraud proof with a minimal trusted base and transparent upgrades.

talks.title: 2024 267 Wear's my Data Understanding the Cross Device Runtime Permission Model in Wearables Dogu
talks.teaser: Explains how permissions on paired phones and Wear OS watches can leak data across devices and confuse users.
talks.summary:
Wearables pair with phones, and Wear OS apps can ask for permissions on either device, yet the talk argues that the two permission models are not truly separate. Once a permission is granted on one device, the data can flow to the other over the pairing channel. The authors built a static taint analysis tool called FlowFinder and ran it on 150 apps. It found cross-device flows in 28 of them, mostly from phone to watch, since many watch faces cannot request permissions on the watch itself.

Manual checks of the apps found that none told users about these flows inside the app, and only one privacy policy stated the type and purpose of the transferred data. Wear OS 2 warned that turning off watch location would stop the watch from using phone location, a claim dropped in Wear OS 3 even though the flows remained. In a user study with 63 Android and Wear OS users, 66% said only the phone app could access phone location after a watch denial, although both apps could. A redirection prompt can also mislead: when the request behind it was camera, more participants wrongly thought the app could not reach photos, media and files.

The authors suggest extra information prompts, a user-centric model where permission decisions sync across devices, and market-level screening with taint analysis. They also note that Android and Wear teams are working on unidirectional synchronization from phone to watch, which was not yet active at the time. The takeaway is that developers should not assume data stays on the device where a permission was granted, and users need clearer disclosure of cross-device sharing.

talks.title: MPCitH without reputation IEEE S^0P online qw gao
talks.teaser: A refined MPC-in-the-head design drops reputation needs and yields fast post-quantum proofs of secret-key knowledge for schemes like Kyber.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with zero-knowledge proofs and the MPC-in-the-head paradigm for constructing non-interactive arguments by simulating multiparty computation and opening randomly chosen participant transcripts. Standard MPC-in-the-head security relies on repeating evaluations many times, so proof size and prover time scale with the security parameter and can become costly for practical use.

The work introduces a protocol referred to as DIET that removes the reputation mechanism from the in-the-head approach and improves efficiency. Shamir secret sharing replaces additive sharing so broadcast shares can be checked on one polynomial, packed secret sharing cuts cost, and a lighter method validates MPC results without full exclusion or Beaver triples in preprocessing. The design supports addition, multiplication, and linear transformation gates so vector-style circuits can be handled; multiplication and related steps gain constant-scale complexity improvements relative to the prior linear dependence on the repetition parameter.

The closing thread is application to proof of knowledge of the secret key for lattice-based post-quantum key encapsulation, where classical signatures do not align cleanly with KEM keys. Efficient proofs matter for certificate-backed deployments such as a post-quantum TLS-style setting. Practitioners should note the trade-off between protocol repetition, sharing structure, and proof size when integrating PQ KEM keys with existing PKI-style ownership proofs.

talks.title: 153 APP Miner Detecting API Misuses via Automatically Mining API Path Patterns Jiasheng Jiang
talks.teaser: Presents a framework that mines API usage path patterns from source code to flag API misuses without predefined templates.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common problem: developers call APIs without knowing their internal mechanics, and breaking the expected usage pattern can open security holes. The speaker gives the example of memory allocation calls that need a size check and a matching free, where a missing check can lead to an overflow and a missing free to a leak. Existing pattern extraction methods rely on hand-written templates, test generation with low coverage, or documentation mining, and many real patterns stay implicit in the source code.

The authors present APMiner, which runs data flow analysis to build control flow graphs and keeps only API calls, condition checks and return statements. Where frequent subgraphs come out disconnected, a topology completion step links them into connected patterns. To keep mining tractable on large codebases, the graphs are encoded in index matrices and processed with an Apriori-style frequent subgraph algorithm. Violations are found by matching each path against the mined patterns with a binary discriminant and ranking the mismatches. In one kernel example, 146 of 147 uses of a time conversion API followed the same overflow check, so the single deviating use was flagged.

Evaluated on four widely used open-source projects, including the Linux kernel, OpenSSL and Apache httpd, the tool extracted 4,788 API path patterns, reported 157 new bugs and found 19 CVEs. The comparison against other tools showed it finding the most true positives. The takeaway for practitioners is that API usage rules can be learned automatically from existing code, without predefined templates.

talks.title: MIMOCrypt Jun Luo John
talks.teaser: MIMOCrypt encrypts Wi-Fi channel state so eavesdroppers lose typing and activity inference while data and approved sensing stay usable.
talks.summary:
Multi-person Wi‑Fi sensing can track activity and infer secrets such as mobile passwords from typing motion alone, without compromising devices. Earlier defenses either protect only a single legitimate sensor or jam everyone, including normal Wi‑Fi users and authorized sensing.

MIMOCrypt targets the physical channel inside the radio rather than short training sequences. Encryption keys ride on OFDM subcarriers and MIMO antennas so over-the-air channel state information looks scrambled to outsiders. Because analog-style encryption distorts recovered signals, the design optimizes keys to hurt eavesdroppers while preserving useful signal quality for communication and approved sensing partners. Sensing clients can adapt via a small key hash that picks among trained encoders instead of receiving the full complex key.

Experiments reported in the talk show prior sensing methods exceeding roughly ninety percent accuracy fall to about sixteen percent under MIMOCrypt for adversaries, with only minor communication bit-error cost. Adding many receive antennas does not reliably break the scheme, since each antenna adds unknown channel and key parameters.
